Die Gegner haben sich u. a. auf U.S.-amerikanische Regierungsbürokratie und Militärs, private Organisationen, Cybersecurity-Unternehmen, Journalisten, die die russische Regierung kritisiert haben, und kritische Infrastruktur-Organisationen konzentriert. Die Energie-Branche war ein besonderes Ziel, wobei mehrere U.S.-amerikanische und internationale Energie-Branche-Netzwerke kompromittiert wurden. Die Akteure nutzen Domains, Hyperlinks und Logon-Seiten gefälschter beliebter Webmail-Dienste, um Sprengangriffe und Wasserhohlstücke durchzuführen. Diese Aktivität hat zumindest seit 2004 angedauert, wobei hervorzuhebende Aktivitäten in 2008, 2017 und 2021 auftraten. Netzwerkschutzbeauftragte sollten ihre Systeme genau beobachten, insbesondere in der Energie-Branche, und regelmäßig ihre Systeme aktualisieren und patchen, um die Bedrohung zu mindern. Robuste Zugriffssteuerungen und Überwachung, sowie Vorsicht bei der Interaktion mit unerbetenen E-Mails oder Hyperlinks, insbesondere von unvertrauten Domains stammen, sind unerlässlich. Diese Kampagne erinnert daran, dass nationale Akteure weiterhin eine Bedrohung für kritische Infrastruktur darstellen und die Wichtigkeit von Vorausschauen in der Abwehrmaßnahmen unverändert ist.

messages.output: The Russian Foreign Intelligence Agency (SVR), the Federal Security Service (FSB) and the General Staff of the Armed Forces (GTsSS) are conducting a campaign targeting Industrial Control Systems (ICS) across multiple industries. The SVR, FSB and GTsSS are using ICS-focused malware to compromise and exploit ICS. The attackers have focused on U.S.-American government bureaucracy and military, private organizations, cybersecurity companies, journalists who have criticized the Russian government, and critical infrastructure organizations. The energy sector was a specific target, with several U.S.-American and international energy sector networks compromised. The actors are using domains, hyperlinks and logon pages of fake popular webmail services to conduct spear attacks and watering hole attacks. This activity has been ongoing at least since 2004, with notable activities in 2008, 2017 and 2021. Network protection officers should closely monitor their systems, especially in the energy sector, and regularly update and patch their systems to mitigate the threat. Robust access controls and monitoring, as well as caution when interacting with unsolicited emails or hyperlinks, especially from untrusted domains, are essential. This campaign serves as a reminder that national actors remain a threat to critical infrastructure and the importance of anticipation in defensive measures remains unchanged.

Text: Cyber threat activity has targeted managed service providers (MSPs) who offer IT services to customers, posing a significant risk to their customers and the overall supply chain. The malicious activity in question is not associated with a specific malware variant, vulnerability, or tactic, technique, or procedure (TTP). As a result, indicators of compromise (IOCs) are not available at this time. MSPs play a critical role in the supply chain, providing IT services and support to their customers. As such, they are prime targets for attackers seeking to exploit vulnerabilities in the supply chain. Attacks targeting MSPs can have a ripple effect, impacting not only the MSP but also its customers who rely on these services. To mitigate this threat, network defenders should take several key steps. First, they should identify and disable any accounts that are no longer in use, as these can be exploited by attackers to gain unauthorized access to the network. Next, network defenders should enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) on MSP accounts that access the customer environment and monitor for unexplained failed authentication attempts. This will help to prevent attackers from using compromised accounts to gain access to the network. Finally, network defenders should ensure that MSP-customer contracts transparently identify ownership of ICT security roles and responsibilities. This will help to prevent misunderstandings or disputes that could compromise security.

The Lazarus Group used AppleJeus trojanized cryptocurrency applications targeting individuals and companies-including cryptocurrency exchanges and financial services companies-through the dissemination of cryptocurrency trading applications that were modified to include malware that facilitates theft of cryptocurrency. As of April 2022, North Korea's Lazarus Group actors have targeted various firms, entities, and exchanges in the blockchain and cryptocurrency industry using spearphishing campaigns and malware to steal cryptocurrency. These actors will likely continue exploiting vulnerabilities of cryptocurrency technology firms, gaming companies, and exchanges to generate and launder funds to support the North Korean regime. Intrusions begin with a large number of spearphishing messages sent to employees of cryptocurrency companies-often working in system administration or software development/IT operations (DevOps)-on a variety of communication platforms. Joint Advisory: Russian State-Sponsored Threat Actors Target U.S. Government and Private Sector Entities

The U.S. government has identified a group of Russian state-sponsored malicious cyber actors, including the FSB, SVR, and GTsSS, who have been actively targeting U.S. government and military personnel, as well as private organizations, cybersecurity companies, and journalists critical of the Russian government. These actors have also been observed targeting U.S. and international Energy Sector networks, critical infrastructure organizations, and private sector organizations.

The threat actors have been using various tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), including the exploitation of domains, hyperlinks, and spoofed popular webmail services' logon pages. This activity is believed to have been ongoing for at least two decades, with the earliest known activity dating back to at least 2004 and continuing through 2021.

The malware used by these threat actors is focused on Industrial Control Systems (ICS), indicating a potential for disrupting critical infrastructure operations. The U.S. government encourages all organizations to increase their cyber resilience against this threat by implementing best practices for identity and access management, protective controls and architecture, and vulnerability and configuration management.

Critical infrastructure organizations are particularly vulnerable to these threat actors, and it is essential that they implement network segmentation to separate network segments based on role and functionality. This can help prevent lateral movement by controlling traffic flows between-and access to-various subnetworks.

The U.S. government also recommends that organizations document incident response procedures in a cyber incident response plan, which should be created and exercised regularly. Additionally, all organizations should be aware of the potential for these threat actors to target their networks and be prepared to respond accordingly.

If you have information on Russian state-sponsored cyber operations targeting U.S. critical infrastructure, contact the Department of State's Rewards for Justice Program. Text: Cyber threat activity has targeted managed service providers (MSPs) who offer IT services to customers, posing a significant risk to their customers and the overall supply chain. The malicious activity in question is not associated with a specific malware variant, vulnerability, or tactic, technique, or procedure (TTP). As a result, indicators of compromise (IOCs) are not available at this time. MSPs play a critical role in the supply chain, providing IT services and support to their customers. As such, they are prime targets for attackers seeking to exploit vulnerabilities in the supply chain. Attacks targeting MSPs can have a ripple effect, impacting not only the MSP but also its customers who rely on these services. To mitigate this threat, network defenders should take several key steps. First, they should identify and disable any accounts that are no longer in use, as these can be exploited by attackers to gain unauthorized access to the network. Next, network defenders should enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) on MSP accounts that access the customer environment and monitor for unexplained failed authentication attempts. This will help to prevent attackers from using compromised accounts to gain access to the network. Finally, network defenders should ensure that MSP-customer contracts transparently identify ownership of ICT security roles and responsibilities. This will help to prevent misunderstandings or disputes that could compromise security.

According to Microsoft, an attacker can send specially crafted packets to one of these operating systems that has RDP enabled. Text: On [Date], our team detected a significant global ransomware campaign targeting Managed Service Providers (MSPs). Initial analysis indicates that the attack is the result of a coordinated effort by malicious cyber actors. The ransomware malware used in the attack spreads rapidly across MSP networks, exploiting vulnerabilities in network configurations and user permissions. Once inside, the malware encrypts sensitive data, rendering it inaccessible to affected parties. The attackers have also been observed using follow-on activity against the MSP's customer base, exacerbating the impact of the incident. Multiple MSPs have reported globally cascading effects, with customers experiencing downtime and data loss. The scope of the attack is significant, with dozens of MSPs and their customers affected worldwide. Our analysis suggests that the attackers are leveraging the MSP's trusted relationship with their customers to spread the malware, making it challenging to detect and contain. Preliminary findings indicate that the attackers are highly sophisticated, with a clear understanding of the MSP's business operations and customer relationships. The use of ransomware as a primary attack vector suggests a focus on financial gain, rather than intellectual property theft or other malicious objectives. Further analysis is required to fully understand the motivations and tactics employed by the attackers, which threaten the MSPs and their customer base.
messages.output: Am [Datum], entdeckte unser Team eine bedeutende globale Ransomware-Kampagne, die sich an Managed Service Providers (MSPs) richtete. Die anfängliche Analyse deutet darauf hin, dass das Angriff Ergebnis eines koordinierten Einsatzes von schädlichen Cyberkriminellen ist. Die bei dem Angriff verwendete Ransomware-Malware verbreitet sich rasch über MSP-Netzwerke, indem sie Schwachstellen in Netzwerk-Konfigurationen und Benutzerberechtigungen ausnutzt. Sobald sie drin sind, verschlüsselt die Malware sensible Daten, was es betroffenen Parteien unmöglich macht, auf sie zuzugreifen. Die Angreifer wurden auch dabei beobachtet, dass sie eine zweite Aktivität gegen die MSP-Kundenbasis durchführen, wodurch sich der Einfluss des Vorfalls verschärfte. Mehrere MSPs berichteten über weltweite Kaskaden von Auswirkungen, wobei Kunden mit Ausfallzeiten und Datenverlust zu kämpfen hatten. Die Reichweite des Angriffs ist erheblich, wobei Dutzende von MSPs und ihre Kunden weltweit betroffen sind. Unsere Analyse deuttet darauf hin, dass die Angreifer den vertrauensvollen Bezug von MSPs zu ihren Kunden ausnutzen, um die Malware zu verbreiten, was es schwierig macht, sie zu erkennen und aufzuhalten. Vorläufige Befunde deuten darauf hin, dass die Angreifer sehr fortgeschritten sind, da sie eine klare Kenntnis der MSP-Unternehmensoperationen und Kundenbeziehungen besitzen. Die Verwendung von Ransomware als primäres Angriffs-Vector deutet darauf hin, dass sich der Schwerpunkt auf finanziellen Gewinn richtet, anstatt auf den Diebstahl von geistigem Eigentum oder andere schädliche Ziele. Weitere Analyse ist erforderlich, um die Motivationen und Taktiken der Angreifer zu verstehen, die die MSPs und ihre Kundenbasis bedrohen.

The timeline of the campaign spans several months, indicating a prolonged and sustained effort by the actors to infiltrate and compromise MSPs. The incident highlights the need for MSPs to implement robust security measures and operational controls to protect against advanced threats. Recommended mitigations include implementing baseline security measures and operational controls, ensuring contractual arrangements specify implementation of measures and controls, and mitigating attack methods such as brute force attacks and phishing. It is also essential for MSPs to store logs for at least six months, implement a segregated logging regime, and implement endpoint detection and network defense monitoring capabilities. Additionally, application allowlisting/denylisting, secure remote access applications, and enforcing multi-factor authentication (MFA) are crucial in preventing unauthorized access to systems and data. Furthermore, reviewing configuration policies to protect against "fail open" and re-enrollment scenarios is critical to preventing the compromise of systems and data. By implementing these mitigations, MSPs can significantly reduce the risk of compromise and protect their customers from advanced threats.

Example 1: Organizations using an HTTPS inspection product should verify that their product properly validates certificate chains and passes any warnings or errors to the client. A partial list of products that may be affected is available at The Risks of SSL Inspection . Organizations may use badssl.com as a method of determining if their preferred HTTPS inspection product properly validates certificates and prevents connections to sites using weak cryptography. At a minimum, if any of the tests in the Certificate section of badssl.com prevent a client with direct Internet access from connecting, those same clients should also refuse the connection when connected to the Internet by way of an HTTPS inspection product. In general, organizations considering the use of HTTPS inspection should carefully consider the pros and cons of such products before implementing . Organizations should also take other steps to secure end-to-end communications, as presented in US-CERT Alert TA15-120A .

Example 2: From at least March 2020 through February 2021, the threat actor connected to the entity via the entity's Pulse Secure VPN appliance ( External Remote Services [ T1133 ]). The threat actor connected via the U.S.-based residential IP addresses listed below, which allowed them to masquerade as teleworking employees. ( Note: these IP addresses belong to routers that are all similar models; based on this activity, CISA suspects that these routers were likely exploited by the threat actor.) The threat actor authenticated to the VPN appliance through several user accounts ( Valid Accounts [ T1078 ]), none of which had multi-factor authentication (MFA) enabled. (CISA does not know how the threat actor initially obtained these credentials.) Once authenticated to the VPN appliance, the threat actor initiated a VPN connection to the environment ( External Remote Services [ T1133 ]). The media access control (MAC) address of the threat actor's machine as recorded in the VPN appliance logs indicates use of a virtual machine. The threat actor then moved laterally to the entity's SolarWinds Orion appliance ( Lateral Movement [ TA0008 ]) and established Persistence [ TA0003 ] by using a PowerShell script (Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell [ T1059.001 ]) to decode ( Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information [ T1140 ]) and install SUPERNOVA ( Ingress Tool Transfer [ T1105 ], Server Software Component: Web Shell [ T1505.003 ]). The SUPERNOVA webshell allows a remote operator to dynamically inject C# source code into a web portal provided via the SolarWinds software suite. The injected code is compiled and directly executed in memory. For more information on SUPERNOVA, refer to MAR-10319053-1.v1 - SUPERNOVA . The threat actor was able to dump credentials from the SolarWinds appliance via two methods ( Credential Access [ TA0006 ]).

Text: Recent investigations have revealed a sophisticated threat campaign orchestrated by Russian state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors. The actors have been targeting Managed Service Providers (MSPs) and their customers, exploiting vulnerabilities in their security posture to gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems and data. The timeline of the campaign spans several months, indicating a prolonged and sustained effort by the actors to infiltrate and compromise MSPs. The incident highlights the need for MSPs to implement robust security measures and operational controls to protect against advanced threats. Recommended mitigations include implementing baseline security measures and operational controls, ensuring contractual arrangements specify implementation of measures and controls, and mitigating attack methods such as brute force attacks and phishing. It is also essential for MSPs to store logs for at least six months, implement a segregated logging regime, and implement endpoint detection and network defense monitoring capabilities. Additionally, application allowlisting/denylisting, secure remote access applications, and enforcing multi-factor authentication (MFA) are crucial in preventing unauthorized access to systems and data. Furthermore, reviewing configuration policies to protect against "fail open" and re-enrollment scenarios is critical to preventing the compromise of systems and data. By implementing these mitigations, MSPs can significantly reduce the risk of compromise and protect their customers from advanced threats.
messages.output: Recente Ermittlungen haben eine sophisticated Bedrohungskampagne aufgedeckt, die von russischen staatlich gesponserten Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)-Akteuren orchestriert wird. Die Akteure haben sich auf Managed Service Providers (MSPs) und deren Kunden konzentriert und dabei Sicherheitslücken in ihrem Sicherheitsposten ausgenutzt, um unerlaubten Zugriff auf sensible Systeme und Daten zu erlangen. Die Zeitlinie der Kampagne umfasst mehrere Monate, was auf eine ausgedehnte und dauerhafte Bemühung der Akteure hinweist, um MSPs zu infiltrieren und zu kompromittieren. Der Vorfall unterstreicht die Notwendigkeit für MSPs, robuste Sicherheitsmaßnahmen und Betriebskontrollen zu implementieren, um sich gegen fortgeschrittene Bedrohungen zu schützen. Empfohlene Abmilderungen umfassen die Implementierung grundlegender Sicherheitsmaßnahmen und Betriebskontrollen, die Sicherstellung, dass vertragliche Vereinbarungen die Implementierung von Maßnahmen und Kontrollen vorsehen, sowie die Abmilderung von Angriffsmethoden wie Angriffen durch Brute-Force-Angriffe und Phishing. Es ist auch unerlässlich für MSPs, Logdateien mindestens sechs Monate aufzubewahren, eine segmentierte Log-Regelung zu implementieren und Überwachungsfunktionen für Endpunkt-Detektion und Netzwerk-Verteidigung zu implementieren. Darüber hinaus ist die Implementierung von Anwendungs-White- und Black-Listen, der Sicherstellung sicheres Remotesupport-Tools und die Durchsetzung von Multi-Faktor-Authentifizierung (MFA) unerlässlich, um unerlaubten Zugriff auf Systeme und Daten zu verhindern. Außerdem ist es entscheidend, Konfigurationsrichtlinien zu überprüfen, um gegen "Fehler, die geöffnet werden" und Wiedereinblendungen zu schützen, um die Komprimierung von Systemen und Daten zu verhindern. Durch die Implementierung dieser Abmilderungen können MSPs das Risiko der Komprimierung deutlich verringern und ihre Kunden vor fortgeschrittenen Bedrohungen schützen.

These actors have been observed targeting ICS/SCADA devices and Windows-based engineering workstations, with a primary focus on compromising and controlling industrial control systems.

Additionally, CISA has identified ASRock motherboard drivers with known vulnerabilities as a potential entry point for these actors. It is essential for organizations in the Energy Sector to be aware of the potential impact of this activity, which includes elevating privileges, moving laterally within an OT environment, and disrupting critical devices or functions.

To mitigate this threat, CISA recommends that organizations take the following steps: Enforce multifactor authentication for all remote access to ICS networks and devices, change all passwords to ICS/SCADA devices and systems on a consistent schedule, and leverage a properly installed continuous OT monitoring solution. CISA encourages all Energy Sector organizations to review their security protocols and take proactive measures to protect their industrial control systems and devices from this emerging threat.

In conjunction with this advisory, CISA has released a detailed analysis of the malicious indicators and behaviors associated with this activity, including YARA signatures that can be used to detect and identify potential threats. Example 1: This file has been identified as CovalentStealer malware. The actor utilized code from several open source projects, including ClientUploader. The retained the internal name "ClientUploader.exe". The program is a file management system that is capable of uploading files to the Internet. When the program is executed, it will spawn an instance of itself in memory called 'koi'. This instance accesses several embedded resources that it uses to locate and manipulate files on the system. The following is a list of the primary embedded resources: ---Begin Embedded Resources--- BaseNetwork - This resource is used to create sessions and establish connections to the server. FileContainer - This resource is used to access file shares via Server Message Block (SMB). It is also used to enumerate files and directories and sort them by Message Digest 5 (MD5) hash. It maintains Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, logins, domain names, passwords, and paths for shares on the network. IFileWorker - This resource is a file management program that is capable of moving and categorizing files. It contains compression libraries for Gzip and Brotli, as well as a file blacklist. Encryption - This resource handles file encryption, decryption and secure communications. It decrypts the configuration file, onedrv.ini (91a8b31c126a021f5c156742016acdcca7d83eac4b583bae5d4fd0a85a96813b) using the hard-coded Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) key 'M(xcHq88q[s=pc7^+u_Gb_}JC%QQwP:h' and an Initialization Vector (IV) using the first half of the AES key (See Figure 1). OneDriveClient - This resource targets a user's OneDrive account and creates an upload session to send the files to a remote server. It is able to access files in the victim's OneDrive by unique ID (See Figure 2). Files are uploaded to a Microsoft Azure client identified in the configuration file onedrv.ini by client ID. ---End Embedded Resources--- The program runs a debugging routine and will output debugging data to a file with the same name as the malware and with the .dat extension, e.g. onedrv.dat (517faa4a0666ec68842f256f08d987935b6ce9ef64e33f027e084e8f45b9366d). Figure 1 - This is the AES encryption routine. The routine uses the hard-coded string 'M(xcHq88q[s=pc7^+u_Gb_}JC%QQwP:h' as the AES key and the first half of the key as the IV.

Example 2: Confirming a successful compromise of ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus may be difficult-the attackers are known to run clean-up scripts designed to remove traces of the initial point of compromise and hide any relationship between exploitation of the vulnerability and the webshell. Note: the domain seed.nkn[.]org is a New Kind of Network (NKN) domain that provides legitimate peer to peer networking services utilizing blockchain technology for decentralization. It is possible to have false positive hits in a corporate network environment and it should be considered suspicious to see any software-initiated contacts to this domain or any subdomain. Organizations that identify any activity related to ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus indicators of compromise within their networks should take action immediately. Zoho ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus build 11306, or higher, fixes CVE-2021-44077. ManageEngine initially released a patch for this vulnerability on September 16, 2021. A subsequent security advisory was released on November 22, 2021, and advised customers to patch immediately. Additional information can be found in the Zoho security advisory released on November 22, 2021 . In addition, Zoho has set up a security response plan center that provides additional details, a downloadable tool that can be run on potentially affected systems, and a remediation guide. FBI and CISA also strongly recommend domain-wide password resets and double Kerberos TGT password resets if any indication is found that the file was compromised. Note: Implementing these password resets should not be taken as a comprehensive mitigation in response to this threat; additional steps may be necessary to regain administrative control of your network. Example 1: On February 5, 2021, unidentified cyber actors obtained unauthorized access to the supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system at a U.S. drinking water treatment facility. The unidentified actors used the SCADA system's software to increase the amount of sodium hydroxide, also known as lye, a caustic chemical, as part of the water treatment process. Water treatment plant personnel immediately noticed the change in dosing amounts and corrected the issue before the SCADA system's software detected the manipulation and alarmed due to the unauthorized change. As a result, the water treatment process remained unaffected and continued to operate as normal. The cyber actors likely accessed the system by exploiting cybersecurity weaknesses, including poor password security, and an outdated operating system. Early information indicates it is possible that a desktop sharing software, such as TeamViewer, may have been used to gain unauthorized access to the system, although this cannot be confirmed at present date. Onsite response to the incident included Pinellas County Sheriff Office (PCSO), U.S. Secret Service (USSS), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Through the course of the investigation, the FBI was not able to confirm that this incident was initiated by a targeted cyber intrusion. The FBI, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) have observed cyber criminals targeting and exploiting desktop sharing software and computer networks running operating systems with end of life status to gain unauthorized access to systems. Desktop sharing software, which has multiple legitimate uses-such as enabling telework, remote technical support, and file transfers-can also be exploited through malicious actors' use of social engineering tactics and other illicit measures. Windows 7 will become more susceptible to exploitation due to lack of security updates and the discovery of new vulnerabilities. Microsoft and other industry professionals strongly recommend upgrading computer systems to an actively supported operating system. Continuing to use any operating system within an enterprise beyond the end of life status may provide cyber criminals access into computer systems.

Example 2: This Joint Cybersecurity Advisory was coauthored by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC), the United Kingdom's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), and the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). This advisory provides details on the top 30 vulnerabilities-primarily Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs)-routinely exploited by malicious cyber actors in 2020 and those being widely exploited thus far in 2021. Cyber actors continue to exploit publicly known-and often dated-software vulnerabilities against broad target sets, including public and private sector organizations worldwide. However, entities worldwide can mitigate the vulnerabilities listed in this report by applying the available patches to their systems and implementing a centralized patch management system. In 2020, cyber actors readily exploited recently disclosed vulnerabilities to compromise unpatched systems. Based on available data to the U.S. Government, a majority of the top vulnerabilities targeted in 2020 were disclosed during the past two years. Cyber actor exploitation of more recently disclosed software flaws in 2020 probably stems, in part, from the expansion of remote work options amid the COVID-19 pandemic. The rapid shift and increased use of remote work options, such as virtual private networks (VPNs) and cloud-based environments, likely placed additional burden on cyber defenders struggling to maintain and keep pace with routine software patching. Four of the most targeted vulnerabilities in 2020 affected remote work, VPNs, or cloud-based technologies. Many VPN gateway devices remained unpatched during 2020, with the growth of remote work options challenging the ability of organizations to conduct rigorous patch management. Vice Society is an intrusion, exfiltration, and extortion hacking group that first appeared in summer 2021. Vice Society actors do not use a ransomware variant of unique origin. Instead, the actors have deployed versions of Hello Kitty/Five Hands and Zeppelin ransomware , but may deploy other variants in the future. Vice Society actors likely obtain initial network access through compromised credentials by exploiting internet-facing applications [ T1190 ]. Prior to deploying ransomware, the actors spend time exploring the network, identifying opportunities to increase accesses, and exfiltrating data [ TA0010 ] for double extortion--a tactic whereby actors threaten to publicly release sensitive data unless a victim pays a ransom. Vice Society actors have been observed using a variety of tools, including SystemBC, PowerShell Empire, and Cobalt Strike to move laterally. They have also used "living off the land" techniques targeting the legitimate Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service [ T1047 ] and tainting shared content [ T1080 ]. Vice Society actors have been observed exploiting the PrintNightmare vulnerability ( CVE-2021-1675 and CVE-2021-34527 ) to escalate privileges [ T1068 ]. To maintain persistence, the criminal actors have been observed leveraging scheduled tasks [ T1053 ], creating undocumented autostart Registry keys [ T1547.001 ], and pointing legitimate services to their custom malicious dynamic link libraries (DLLs) through a tactic known as DLL side-loading [ T1574.002 ]. Vice Society actors attempt to evade detection through masquerading their malware and tools as legitimate files [ T1036 ], using process injection [ T1055 ], and likely use evasion techniques to defeat automated dynamic analysis [ T1497 ]. Example 1: Best Practices • Apply patches as soon as possible • Disable unnecessary ports and protocols • Replace end-of-life infrastructure • Implement a centralized patch management system This joint Cybersecurity Advisory describes the ways in which People's Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored cyber actors continue to exploit publicly known vulnerabilities in order to establish a broad network of compromised infrastructure. These actors use the network to exploit a wide variety of targets worldwide, including public and private sector organizations. The advisory details the targeting and compromise of major telecommunications companies and network service providers and the top vulnerabilities-primarily Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs)-associated with network devices routinely exploited by the cyber actors since 2020. This joint Cybersecurity Advisory was coauthored by the National Security Agency (NSA), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). It builds on previous NSA, CISA, and FBI reporting to inform federal and state, local, tribal, and territorial (SLTT) government; critical infrastructure (CI), including the Defense Industrial Base (DIB); and private sector organizations about notable trends and persistent tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). Entities can mitigate the vulnerabilities listed in this advisory by applying the available patches to their systems, replacing end-of-life infrastructure, and implementing a centralized patch management program. NSA, CISA, and the FBI urge U.S. and allied governments, CI, and private industry organizations to apply the recommendations listed in the Mitigations section and Appendix A: Vulnerabilities to increase their defensive posture and reduce the risk of PRC state-sponsored malicious cyber actors affecting their critical networks.

Example 2: US-CERT has received multiple reports of Petya ransomware infections in many countries around the world. Ransomware is a type of malicious software that infects a computer and restricts users' access to the infected machine until a ransom is paid to unlock it. Individuals and organizations are discouraged from paying the ransom, as this does not guarantee that access will be restored. Using unpatched and unsupported software may increase the risk of proliferation of cybersecurity threats, such as ransomware. Petya ransomware encrypts the master boot records of infected Windows computers, making affected machines unusable. Open-source reports indicate that the ransomware exploits vulnerabilities in Server Message Block (SMB). US-CERT encourages users and administrators to review the US-CERT article on the Microsoft SMBv1 Vulnerability and the Microsoft Security Bulletin MS17-010 . For additional information on Petya, review US-CERT Alert TA16-181A . Please report any ransomware incidents to the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) .

Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: According to information derived from FBI investigations, malicious cyber actors are increasingly using a style of brute force attack known as password spraying against organizations in the United States and abroad. On February 2018, the Department of Justice in the Southern District of New York, indicted nine Iranian nationals, who were associated with the Mabna Institute, for computer intrusion offenses related to activity described in this report. The techniques and activity described herein, while characteristic of Mabna actors, are not limited solely to use by this group. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) are releasing this Alert to provide further information on this activity. In a traditional brute-force attack, a malicious actor attempts to gain unauthorized access to a single account by guessing the password. This can quickly result in a targeted account getting locked-out, as commonly used account-lockout policies allow three to five bad attempts during a set period of time. During a password-spray attack (also known as the "low-and-slow" method), the malicious actor attempts a single password against many accounts before moving on to attempt a second password, and so on. This technique allows the actor to remain undetected by avoiding rapid or frequent account lockouts. Password spray campaigns typically target single sign-on (SSO) and cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols. An actor may target this specific protocol because federated authentication can help mask malicious traffic. Additionally, by targeting SSO applications, malicious actors hope to maximize access to intellectual property during a successful compromise. Email applications are also targeted. In those instances, malicious actors would have the ability to utilize inbox synchronization to (1) obtain unauthorized access to the organization's email directly from the cloud, (2) subsequently download user mail to locally stored email files, (3) identify the entire company's email address list, and/or (4) surreptitiously implements inbox rules for the forwarding of sent and received messages. A successful network intrusion can have severe impacts, particularly if the compromise becomes public and sensitive information is exposed. Possible impacts include:

Example 2: After gaining initial access, the actors exploit CVE-2020-1472 to compromise all Active Directory (AD) identity services. Actors have then been observed using legitimate remote access tools, such as VPN and Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), to access the environment with the compromised credentials. Observed activity targets multiple sectors and is not limited to SLTT entities. CISA recommends network staff and administrators review internet-facing infrastructure for these and similar vulnerabilities that have or could be exploited to a similar effect, including Juniper CVE-2020-1631 , Pulse Secure CVE-2019-11510 , Citrix NetScaler CVE-2019-19781 , and Palo Alto Networks CVE-2020-2021 (this list is not considered exhaustive). APT threat actors are actively leveraging legacy vulnerabilities in internet-facing infrastructure ( Exploit Public-Facing Application [ T1190 ], External Remote Services [ T1133 ]) to gain initial access into systems. The APT actors appear to have predominately gained initial access via the Fortinet FortiOS VPN vulnerability CVE-2018-13379 . Although not observed in this campaign, other vulnerabilities, listed below, could be used to gain network access (as analysis is evolving, these listed vulnerabilities should not be considered comprehensive). As a best practice, it is critical to patch all known vulnerabilities within internet-facing infrastructure. CVE-2018-13379 is a path traversal vulnerability in the FortiOS SSL VPN web portal. An unauthenticated attacker could exploit this vulnerability to download FortiOS system files through specially crafted HTTP resource requests. CVE-2020-15505 is a remote code execution vulnerability in MobileIron Core & Connector versions 10.3 and earlier. This vulnerability allows an external attacker, with no privileges, to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system. As mobile device management (MDM) systems are critical to configuration management for external devices, they are usually highly permissioned and make a valuable target for threat actors. Post initial access, the APT actors use multiple techniques to expand access to the environment. The actors are leveraging CVE-2020-1472 in Windows Netlogon to escalate privileges and obtain access to Windows AD servers. Actors are also leveraging the opensource tools such as Mimikatz and the CrackMapExec tool to obtain valid account credentials from AD servers ( Valid Accounts [ T1078 ]).

Example 1: A recent report, The Security Impact of HTTPS Interception , highlighted several security concerns with HTTPS inspection products and outlined survey results of these issues. Many HTTPS inspection products do not properly verify the certificate chain of the server before re-encrypting and forwarding client data, allowing the possibility of a MiTM attack. Furthermore, certificate-chain verification errors are infrequently forwarded to the client, leading a client to believe that operations were performed as intended with the correct server. This report provided a method to allow servers to detect clients that are having their traffic manipulated by HTTPS inspection products. The website badssl.com is a resource where clients can verify whether their HTTPS inspection products are properly verifying certificate chains. Clients can also use this site to verify whether their HTTPS inspection products are enabling connections to websites that a browser or other client would otherwise reject. For example, an HTTPS inspection product may allow deprecated protocol versions or weak ciphers to be used between itself and a web server. Because client systems may connect to the HTTPS inspection product using strong cryptography, the user will be unaware of any weakness on the other side of the HTTPS inspection. Because the HTTPS inspection product manages the protocols, ciphers, and certificate chain, the product must perform the necessary HTTPS validations. Failure to perform proper validation or adequately convey the validation status increases the probability that the client will fall victim to MiTM attacks by malicious third parties.

Example 1: In September 2015, an attack known as SYNful Knock was disclosed. SYNful Knock silently changes a router's operating system image, thus allowing attackers to gain a foothold on a victim's network. The malware can be customized and updated once embedded. When the modified malicious image is uploaded, it provides a backdoor into the victim's network. Using a crafted TCP SYN packet, a communication channel is established between the compromised device and the malicious command and control (C2) server. The impact of this infection to a network or device is severe and most likely indicates that there may be additional backdoors or compromised devices on the network. This foothold gives an attacker the ability to maneuver and infect other hosts and access sensitive data. The initial infection vector does not leverage a zero-day vulnerability. Attackers either use the default credentials to log into the device or obtain weak credentials from other insecure devices or communications. The implant resides within a modified IOS image and, when loaded, maintains its persistence in the environment, even after a system reboot. Any further modules loaded by the attacker will only exist in the router's volatile memory and will not be available for use after the device reboots. However, these devices are rarely or never rebooted. To prevent the size of the image from changing, the malware overwrites several legitimate IOS functions with its own executable code. The attacker examines the functionality of the router and determines functions that can be overwritten without causing issues on the router. Thus, the overwritten functions will vary upon deployment. The attacker can utilize the secret backdoor password in three different authentication scenarios. In these scenarios the implant first checks to see if the user input is the backdoor password. If so, access is granted. Otherwise, the implanted code will forward the credentials for normal verification of potentially valid credentials. This generally raises the least amount of suspicion. Cisco has provided an alert on this attack vector. For more information, see the Cisco SYNful Knock Security Advisory .

Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: In September 2015, an attack known as SYNful Knock was disclosed. SYNful Knock silently changes a router's operating system image, thus allowing attackers to gain a foothold on a victim's network. The malware can be customized and updated once embedded. When the modified malicious image is uploaded, it provides a backdoor into the victim's network. Using a crafted TCP SYN packet, a communication channel is established between the compromised device and the malicious command and control (C2) server. The impact of this infection to a network or device is severe and most likely indicates that there may be additional backdoors or compromised devices on the network. This foothold gives an attacker the ability to maneuver and infect other hosts and access sensitive data. The initial infection vector does not leverage a zero-day vulnerability. Attackers either use the default credentials to log into the device or obtain weak credentials from other insecure devices or communications. The implant resides within a modified IOS image and, when loaded, maintains its persistence in the environment, even after a system reboot. Any further modules loaded by the attacker will only exist in the router's volatile memory and will not be available for use after the device reboots. However, these devices are rarely or never rebooted. To prevent the size of the image from changing, the malware overwrites several legitimate IOS functions with its own executable code. The attacker examines the functionality of the router and determines functions that can be overwritten without causing issues on the router. Thus, the overwritten functions will vary upon deployment. The attacker can utilize the secret backdoor password in three different authentication scenarios. In these scenarios the implant first checks to see if the user input is the backdoor password. If so, access is granted. Otherwise, the implanted code will forward the credentials for normal verification of potentially valid credentials. This generally raises the least amount of suspicion. Cisco has provided an alert on this attack vector. For more information, see the Cisco SYNful Knock Security Advisory .

Example 2: Enable multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts: Azure Active Directory (AD) Global Administrators in an O365 environment have the highest level of administrator privileges at the tenant level. This is equivalent to the Domain Administrator in an on-premises AD environment. The Azure AD Global Administrators are the first accounts created so that administrators can begin configuring their tenant and eventually migrate their users. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is not enabled by default for these accounts. Microsoft has moved towards a "Secure by default" model, but even this must be enabled by the customer. The new feature, called "Security Defaults," assists with enforcing administrators' usage of MFA. These accounts are internet accessible because they are hosted in the cloud. If not immediately secured, an attacker can compromise these cloud-based accounts and maintain persistence as a customer migrates users to O365. Assign Administrator roles using Role-based Access Control (RBAC): Given its high level of default privilege, you should only use the Global Administrator account when absolutely necessary. Instead, using Azure AD's numerous other built-in administrator roles instead of the Global Administrator account can limit assigning of overly permissive privileges to legitimate administrators. Practicing the principle of "Least Privilege" can greatly reduce the impact if an administrator account is compromised. Always assign administrators only the minimum permissions they need to do conduct their tasks. Enable Unified Audit Log (UAL): O365 has a logging capability called the Unified Audit Log that contains events from Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, OneDrive, Azure AD, Microsoft Teams, PowerBI, and other O365 services. An administrator must enable the Unified Audit Log in the Security and Compliance Center before queries can be run. Enabling UAL allows administrators the ability to investigate and search for actions within O365 that could be potentially malicious or not within organizational policy.

Text: On [date], our organization suffered a ransomware attack attributed to the Vice Society actor, who leveraged known vulnerabilities and exploited network weaknesses to gain unauthorized access. The attackers used the Hello Kitty/Five Hands and Zeppelin malware variants, which are associated with the group and have been linked to previous ransomware campaigns. The Vice Society actor exploited two vulnerabilities to carry out the attack: CVE-2021-1675: A vulnerability in the Apache Log4j library that allowed the attackers to execute arbitrary code on compromised systems. CVE-2021-34527: A vulnerability in the Microsoft Defender for Cloud protection service that was used to disable security features and allow malware to spread. The attackers employed various techniques to achieve their objectives, including: T1190: Exploiting phishing emails to distribute malware and gain initial access. T1047: Synchronizing data between compromised systems to facilitate lateral movement. T1068: Executing commands and scripts to carry out post-exploitation activities. T1053: Creating new user accounts to maintain persistence. T1547.001: Using web shells to maintain a persistent presence on compromised systems. T1036: Using scheduled tasks to execute malicious activities. T1055: Collecting system information to enhance the attackers' understanding of the network. T1497: Using the compromised systems to launch attacks on other targets. T1574.002: Leveraging WMI to collect sensitive information. T107: Other (TTPs listed but not explained in detail) T1053, T1055: Collecting system information and creating new user accounts to maintain persistence. The impact of the attack was significant, with the attackers demanding a ransom in exchange for restoring access to compromised systems. The use of double extortion tactics highlights the group's willingness to destroy data if their demands are not met. Our mitigation recommendations include: Using strong credentials for all users and accounts. Applying patches for known vulnerabilities in a timely manner. Monitoring network activity closely for signs of malicious activity. Using anti-malware software to detect and prevent malware infections.

Example 1: PRC state-sponsored cyber actors readily exploit vulnerabilities to compromise unpatched network devices. Network devices, such as Small Office/Home Office (SOHO) routers and Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices, serve as additional access points to route command and control (C2) traffic and act as midpoints to conduct network intrusions on other entities. Over the last few years, a series of high-severity vulnerabilities for network devices provided cyber actors with the ability to regularly exploit and gain access to vulnerable infrastructure devices. In addition, these devices are often overlooked by cyber defenders, who struggle to maintain and keep pace with routine software patching of Internet-facing services and endpoint devices. Since 2020, PRC state-sponsored cyber actors have conducted widespread campaigns to rapidly exploit publicly identified security vulnerabilities, also known as common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs). This technique has allowed the actors to gain access into victim accounts using publicly available exploit code against virtual private network (VPN) services [ T1133 ] or public facing applications [ T1190 ]-without using their own distinctive or identifying malware-so long as the actors acted before victim organizations updated their systems. Text: Network defenders should be aware of a recent surge in activity by a diverse range of threat actors targeting critical infrastructure and Operational Technology/Industrial Control Systems (OT/ICS) assets. Threat actors including nation-state actors, cyber criminals, state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors, independent hackers, and insider threats have been observed attempting to compromise power grids, water treatment facilities, and dams using ransomware as a common tool. The ultimate goals of these actors may extend beyond financial gain, with some aiming to destabilize economic landscapes, support broader military campaigns, or inflict psychological or social impacts on a population. The consequences of these attacks can have far-reaching effects on public confidence in critical infrastructure. The targeting of OT/ICS assets by these threat actors is of particular concern, as successful compromises of these systems can have catastrophic consequences for public safety and economic stability. Network defenders must therefore remain vigilant in their monitoring of systems and networks, prepared to rapidly respond to potential threats. A comprehensive understanding of threat actor motivations and tactics is essential for developing effective defense strategies. This includes accounting for both the technical requirements for protecting OT/ICS assets and the human element, where insider threats can pose a significant risk. Organizations should consider implementing robust access controls, auditing, and monitoring to prevent insider threats, as well as conducting regular training and awareness campaigns to educate employees on the importance of security best practices.

Bedrohungsbefrager einschließlich Staatenbundesstaatlicher Bedrohungsbefrager, Cyberkrimineller, staatlich gesponserten fortschrittlicher anhaltender Bedrohungen (APTs), unabhängiger Hacker und Insiderbedrohungen wurden beobachtet, wie sie mit Ransomware versuchen, Kraftwerke, Wasserversorgungsanlagen und Stauseen zu kompromittieren. Die letztendlichen Ziele dieser Befrager können über den finanziellen Gewinn hinausgehen, da einige versuchen, wirtschaftliche Landschaften zu destabilisieren, umgekehrte militärische Kampagnen zu unterstützen oder psychologische oder soziale Auswirkungen auf eine Bevölkerung herbeizuführen. Die Folgen dieser Angriffe können weitreichende Auswirkungen auf das öffentliche Vertrauen in kritische Infrastrukturen haben. Die Zielauswahl von OT/ICS-Asseten durch diese Befrager ist von besonderem Anlass, da erfolgreiche Komprimierungen dieser Systeme katastrophale Folgen für die öffentliche Sicherheit und wirtschaftliche Stabilität haben können. Netzsicherheitsbeauftragte müssen also stets wachsam in der Überwachung von Systemen und Netzwerken bleiben und bereit sein, potenzielle Bedrohungen schnell zu beantworten. Text: This incident report details a malicious activity involving the TRITON malware, a highly sophisticated malware known to be used by nation-state actors. The malware has been observed targeting control systems, specifically targeting programmable logic controllers (PLCs) from various manufacturers, including Triconex, Schneider Electric, and OMRON, as well as Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture (OPC UA) servers. The tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) employed by the actors involved in this incident are consistent with those used by groups with limited means. The actors leveraged a range of techniques, including developing or purchasing custom tools, leveraging resident system utilities, and using available exploitation tools. The impact of this malicious activity was significant, with the goal of disabling the safety system. This suggests that the actors were attempting to compromise the integrity of the control systems, potentially leading to catastrophic consequences. To prevent similar incidents in the future, we recommend implementing secure remote access protocols and limiting remote access capabilities. Regularly updating PLCs and control systems with the latest security patches and properly configuring systems to prevent unauthorized access are also crucial.

Das Malware-Programm ist darauf ausgelegt, Kontrollsysteme anzugreifen, insbesondere Zielsetzung auf programmierbare Logik-Controller (PLC) von verschiedenen Herstellern, einschließlich Triconex, Schneider Electric und OMRON sowie Open-Platform-Communications- Unified-Architecture-(OPC-UA)-Server. Der Einfluss dieser schädlichen Aktivität war erheblich, da der Zweck darin bestand, das Sicherheitssystem zu deaktivieren. Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: On January 3, 2018, the National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center (NCCIC) became aware of a set of security vulnerabilities-known as Meltdown and Spectre -that affect modern computer processors. These vulnerabilities can be exploited to steal sensitive data present in a computer systems' memory. CPU hardware implementations are vulnerable to side-channel attacks, referred to as Meltdown and Spectre. Meltdown is a bug that "melts" the security boundaries normally enforced by the hardware, affecting desktops, laptops, and cloud computers. Spectre is a flaw an attacker can exploit to force a program to reveal its data. The name derives from "speculative execution"-an optimization method a computer system performs to check whether it will work to prevent a delay when actually executed. Spectre affects almost all devices including desktops, laptops, cloud servers, and smartphones. An attacker can gain access to the system by establishing command and control presence on a machine via malicious Javascript, malvertising, or phishing. Once successful, the attacker could escalate privileges to exploit Meltdown and Spectre vulnerabilities, revealing sensitive information from a computer's kernel memory, including keystrokes, passwords, encryption keys, and other valuable information. NCCIC encourages users and administrators to refer to their hardware and software vendors for the most recent information. In the case of Spectre, the vulnerability exists in CPU architecture rather than in software, and is not easily patched; however, this vulnerability is more difficult to exploit. After patching, performance impacts may vary, depending on use cases. NCCIC recommends administrators ensure that performance is monitored for critical applications and services, and work with their vendor(s) and service provider(s) to mitigate the effect, if possible. Additionally, NCCIC recommends users and administrators who rely on cloud infrastructure work with their CSP to mitigate and resolve any impacts resulting from host OS patching and mandatory rebooting.

Example 2: Note: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) is part of an ongoing #StopRansomware effort to publish advisories for network defenders that detail various ransomware variants and ransomware threat actors. These #StopRansomware advisories include recently and historically observed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and indicators of compromise (IOCs) to help organizations protect against ransomware. Visit stopransomware.gov to see all #StopRansomware advisories and to learn more about other ransomware threats and no-cost resources. Actions to take today to mitigate cyber threats from ransomware: • Prioritize and remediate known exploited vulnerabilities . • Train users to recognize and report phishing attempts. • Enable and enforce multifactor authentication. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), and the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center (MS-ISAC) are releasing this joint CSA to disseminate IOCs and TTPs associated with Vice Society actors identified through FBI investigations as recently as September 2022. The FBI, CISA, and the MS-ISAC have recently observed Vice Society actors disproportionately targeting the education sector with ransomware attacks. After obtaining access, the Russian government cyber actors conducted network reconnaissance, moved laterally, and collected information pertaining to Industrial Control Systems (ICS). Analysis by DHS and FBI, resulted in the identification of distinct indicators and behaviors related to this activity. Of note, the report Dragonfly: Western energy sector targeted by sophisticated attack group, released by Symantec on September 6, 2017, provides additional information about this ongoing campaign. This campaign comprises two distinct categories of victims: staging and intended targets. The initial victims are peripheral organizations such as trusted third-party suppliers with less secure networks, referred to as "staging targets" throughout this alert. The threat actors used the staging targets' networks as pivot points and malware repositories when targeting their final intended victims. NCCIC and FBI judge the ultimate objective of the actors is to compromise organizational networks, also referred to as the "intended target." CISA had not observed the threat actor using privileged accounts prior to the credential dumps, and the acc­­ount being used to connect to the SolarWinds appliance (via VPN) did not have sufficient privilege to access it. The PowerShell process that initiated the credential harvesting and installation of SUPERNOVA was a child process of the process. ( Note: although the threat actor likely exploited CVE-2020-10148, it could have also exploited another API authentication bypass or remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability.) Several weeks later, the threat actor connected again via the VPN appliance and attempted to use credentials gained from the SolarWinds appliance. The threat actor connected to one machine via Server Message Block (SMB) (Transmission Control Protocol [TCP] port 445) and then attempted to login to an additional workstation ( Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares [ T1021.002 ]). No additional activity was observed during this session.

Initial analysis reveals a combination of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) employed to gain unauthorized access. The threat actors used Mimikatz and Ngrok malware. Mimikatz is a credential stealer that extracts Windows authentication credentials from memory, while Ngrok is a reverse tunneling tool for bypassing firewalls and establishing command and control (C2) communication. They attempted to evade detection by clearing security logs (T1018) and concealing their activities (T1003.001). To mitigate the incident, we implemented additional anti-virus measures, changed the password for the local administrator account, and are closely monitoring the network for lateral movement.

Example 1: JexBoss is a tool used to test and exploit vulnerabilities in Java applications and platforms, including the JBoss AS/WildFly web server framework. JexBoss is written in the Python programming language using standard Python libraries. JexBoss is run from the command-line interface (CLI) and operated using a console interface. JexBoss was released as an open-source tool on GitHub in November 2014. JexBoss' author regularly added new features and exploits until March 2017. Early versions of JexBoss specifically targeted JBoss AS versions 3-6. JexBoss has since evolved into a framework that can be used to test and exploit generic Java-related vulnerabilities over HyperText Transfer Protocol (HTTP). In addition to testing JBoss AS for weak default configurations, JexBoss includes exploits for a variety of known vulnerabilities in Java-based frameworks, including some versions of Java Server Faces, Java Seam Framework, Remote Method Invocation over HTTP, Jenkins CLI, Remote Java Management Extension (JMX), and Apache Struts. JexBoss also offers attackers the ability to target deserialization vulnerabilities in generic Java applications and servlets by allowing an attacker to specifically target Uniform Resource Locators (URLs) and parameters. This capability can help attackers customize their attacks against their target and exploit zero-day Java deserialization vulnerabilities. JexBoss' ultimate goal is to provide the attacker with a means of executing arbitrary operating system (OS) commands on the target host. This is achieved by using one of the following mechanisms: JBoss AS/WildFly is a Java-based web server framework that simplifies the process of installing, deploying, and maintaining servlets. JBoss AS was released in 2002 as JBoss AS version 3 and was under continued development until 2012, with the final release of JBoss AS 7.1.1. JBoss AS 7.1.1 was then rebranded under the community project WildFly, which remains under continued development and maintenance. Legacy versions of JBoss AS (particularly versions 6 and older) have unpatched security vulnerabilities because they are no longer maintained. In August 2018, NCCIC's search via the Shodan search engine showed at least 28,060 web servers running outdated and unsupported JBoss AS software.

**Threat Actors Utilizing Mimikatz and Ngrok to Achieve Lateral Movement**

Threat actors have been observed utilizing Mimikatz and Ngrok to compromise enterprise networks and achieve lateral movement. These threat actors have been employing tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems and data.

**TTPs:**

The threat actors have been observed employing the following TTPs:

* **T1018: System Information Discovery**: The threat actors have been using Mimikatz to gather system information, including system configuration, user accounts, and network settings.

* **T1136.002: Command and Control (C2) – Commonly Used Port**: The threat actors have been using Ngrok to establish C2 connections on commonly used ports.
* **T1098: Application Dependent Command and Control**: The threat actors have been using Mimikatz to execute application-dependent commands and control the compromised systems.
* **T1003.001: OS Credential Dumping**: The threat actors have been using Mimikatz to dump Windows credentials and gain unauthorized access to sensitive systems.

**Indicators of Compromise (IOCs):**

The following IOCs have been identified:

* Presence of Mimikatz and Ngrok on the compromised system
* Unusual network activity, including proxy connections and C2 communications
* System information discovery and credential dumping

**Mitigations:**

To prevent compromise, we recommend implementing the following mitigations:

* Implementing additional anti-virus software and keeping it up-to-date
* Changing passwords for the local administrator account
* Monitoring for lateral movement and suspicious network activity

**Recommendations:**

We recommend that all organizations take immediate action to assess their network and systems for potential compromise. Regularly updating anti-virus software, changing passwords for sensitive accounts, and monitoring for suspicious activity can help prevent lateral movement and compromise.

Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: According to numerous open-source reports, a widespread ransomware campaign is affecting various organizations with reports of tens of thousands of infections in over 150 countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Spain, Russia, Taiwan, France, and Japan. The software can run in as many as 27 different languages. The latest version of this ransomware variant, known as WannaCry, WCry, or Wanna Decryptor, was discovered the morning of May 12, 2017, by an independent security researcher and has spread rapidly over several hours, with initial reports beginning around 4:00 AM EDT, May 12, 2017. Open-source reporting indicates a requested ransom of .1781 bitcoins, roughly $300 U.S. This Alert is the result of efforts between the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center (NCCIC) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to highlight known cyber threats. DHS and the FBI continue to pursue related information of threats to federal, state, and local government systems and as such, further releases of technical information may be forthcoming. Initial reports indicate the hacker or hacking group behind the WannaCry campaign is gaining access to enterprise servers through the exploitation of a critical Windows SMB vulnerability. Microsoft released a security update for the MS17-010 vulnerability on March 14, 2017. Additionally, Microsoft released patches for Windows XP, Windows 8, and Windows Server 2003 operating systems on May 13, 2017. See TA17-132A_WannaCry.xlsx and TA17-132A_WannaCry_stix.xml for IOCs developed immediately after WannaCry ransomware appeared. These links contain identical content in two different formats. Three files were submitted to US-CERT for analysis. All files are confirmed as components of a ransomware campaign identified as "WannaCry", a.k.a "WannaCrypt" or ".wnCry". The first file is a dropper, which contains and runs the ransomware, propagating via the MS17-010/EternalBlue SMBv1.0 exploit. The remaining two files are ransomware components containing encrypted plug-ins responsible for encrypting the victim users files. For a list of IOCs found during analysis, see the STIX file. This artifact (5bef35496fcbdbe841c82f4d1ab8b7c2) is a malicious PE32 executable that has been identified as a WannaCry ransomware dropper. Upon execution, the dropper attempts to connect to the following hard-coded URI:

Example 2: Analysts suspect the malware targets insecure or unsecured user accounts and spreads through poorly secured network shares. Once the malware establishes unauthorized access on the victim's systems, it communicates information about victim's systems to HIDDEN COBRA actors using malicious email addresses. This information includes the IP address and host name-as well as the username and password-of each victim's system. HIDDEN COBRA actors can use this information to remotely access a compromised system via the SMB protocol. This alert's IOC files provide HIDDEN COBRA IOCs related to Joanap and Brambul. DHS and FBI recommend that network administrators review the information provided, identify whether any of the provided IP addresses fall within their organizations' allocated IP address space, and-if found-take necessary measures to remove the malware. When reviewing network perimeter logs for the IP addresses, organizations may find instances of these IP addresses attempting to connect to their systems. Upon reviewing the traffic from these IP addresses, system owners may find some traffic relates to malicious activity and some traffic relates to legitimate activity.

According to open-source reports, a ransomware campaign attributed to Hive actors is affecting organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health (HPH) sector. The malware, known as Hive ransomware, has been identified as a significant threat, with reports of infections in multiple countries. The latest version of the Hive ransomware variant was discovered through collaborative efforts between cybersecurity researchers and has spread rapidly, with initial reports emerging over the past several weeks.

This Alert is the result of a joint effort between the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center (NCCIC) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) to highlight known cyber threats. DHS and the FBI continue to pursue related information on threats to federal, state, and local government systems and may release additional technical information in the future.

Initial reports indicate that the Hive ransomware campaign is spreading through the exploitation of insecure or unsecured user accounts and poorly secured network shares. Once the malware gains unauthorized access to a victim's system, it communicates information about the system to Hive actors using malicious email addresses. This information includes the IP address and host name, as well as the username and password, of each victim's system.

To mitigate the threat, DHS and the FBI recommend that network administrators review the information provided and identify whether any of the provided IP addresses fall within their organizations' allocated IP address space. If found, they should take necessary measures to remove the malware. Additionally, administrators are advised to remove any application not deemed necessary for day-to-day operations, implement measures to limit potential adversarial use of common system and network discovery techniques, and apply recommendations to prepare for, mitigate/prevent, and respond to ransomware incidents.

See the attached IOC files for indicators related to the Hive ransomware campaign. These files contain indicators that may be used to identify and block malicious activity.

Text: This advisory alerts network defenders to the ongoing threat posed by Hive actors, a group known to employ the Hive ransomware variant in attacks against the Healthcare and Public Health (HPH) sector. The Hive actors' primary objective is to extort payments from targeted organizations by encrypting sensitive data and threatening to expose it unless a ransom is paid. Network defenders should be aware that the Hive actors' tactics include using the Hive ransomware variant and exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in software and systems. They also leverage publicly available tools and techniques to facilitate the attack. In some cases, the actors may use social engineering tactics to gain initial access to the network. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) associated with Hive ransomware attacks include suspicious network connections to unknown or untrusted IP addresses. Network defenders should also monitor for unusual activity related to remote access tools, such as RDP. To mitigate the risk of a Hive ransomware attack, network defenders should take the following steps. Remove any application not deemed necessary for day-to-day operations to limit the attack surface. Implement measures to limit potential adversarial use of common system and network discovery techniques, such as network scanning and enumeration. Finally, apply recommendations to prepare for, mitigate/prevent, and respond to ransomware incidents, including conducting regular backups and developing incident response plans.
messages.output: Dieses Warnung benachrichtigt Netzwerkverteidiger über die anhaltende Bedrohung durch Hive-Aktivitäten, eine Gruppe, die bekanntschaftlich das Hive-Ransomware-Modell bei Angriffen auf das Gesundheits- und Öffentlichkeitswesen-Sektor (HPH) verwendet. Das Hauptziel der Hive-Aktivitäten besteht darin, Zahlungen von Zielsorganisationen durch Verschlüsselung empfindlicher Daten und Bedrohung ihrer Offenlegung, es sei denn, eine Zahlung wird gefordert. Netzwerkverteidiger sollten sich bewusst sein, dass die Taktiken der Hive-Aktivitäten den Einsatz des Hive-Ransomware-Modells und die Ausbeutung nicht gepatcheter Schwachstellen in Software und Systemen einschließen. Sie nutzen auch öffentlich verfügbare Werkzeuge und Techniken, um den Angriff zu erleichtern. In einigen Fällen können die Aktivitäten soziale Ingenieursangriffe verwenden, um den Zugriff auf das Netzwerk zu erlangen. Indikatoren der Kompromittierung (IOCs), die mit Angriffen des Hive-Ransomware-Modells verbunden sind, umfassen verdächtige Netzwerkverbindungen zu unbekannten oder nicht vertrauenswürdigen IP-Adressen. Netzwerkverteidiger sollten auch die ungewöhnliche Aktivität beobachten, die mit entferntem Zugriffswerkzeugen wie RDP verbunden ist. Um die Gefahr eines Angriffs durch das Hive-Ransomware-Modell zu mindern, sollten Netzwerkverteidiger die folgenden Schritte unternehmen. Entfernen Sie alle Anwendungen, die für die laufenden Betriebsanforderungen nicht notwendig sind, um den Angriffsbereich zu begrenzen. Implementieren Sie Maßnahmen zur Begrenzung des potenziellen Einsatzes der Gruppe durch gemeinsame System- und Netzwerkentdeckungstechniken, wie Netzwerkskanning und Enumeration. Abschließend sollten Anwendungen zur Vorbereitung, Begrenzung/Verhinderung und Beantwortung von Ransomware-Angriffen empfohlen werden, einschließlich regelmäßiger Backup-Aufzeichnungen und der Entwicklung von Verteidigungswplanen.

Netzwerkverteidiger sollten sich der Indikatoren für den Vertrauensbruch (IOCs) bewusst sein, die mit dieser Aktivität verbunden sind, da der Fokus des Akteurs auf das Zugreifen und Ausnutzen von sensiblen Informationen darauf hindeutet, dass die Ansätze des Akteurs für eine gezielte und fortschrittliche Vorgehensweise entwickelt wurden. Die Taktiken, Techniken und Verfahren (TTPs) des Akteurs scheinen auf eine langfristige Zugriffsmöglichkeit auf gefährdete Systeme ausgerichtet zu sein, was die Abführung sensibler Daten ermöglicht. Dies führte zu einer nicht autorisierten Zugriffsmöglichkeit und Privilegien über sehr sensible Informationen. Um dieses Risiko zu mindern, sollten Netzwerkverteidiger daran denken, Sicherheitsanforderungen für das Härten zu implementieren, um die Ausnutzung bekannter Sicherheitslücken zu verhindern. Die forensische Analyse von betroffenen Systemen könnte ebenfalls notwendig sein, um die Auswirkungen der Aktivitäten des Akteurs zu identifizieren und zu beheben. Darüber hinaus könnte das CISA-Hunt- und -Incident-Response-Programm (CHIRP) möglicherweise Unterstützung bei der Identifizierung und Verarbeitung potenzieller Vorfälle anbieten, die mit dieser Aktivität zusammenhängen. Netzwerkverteidiger sollten wachsam bleiben und zusätzliche Sicherheitsmaßnahmen in Betracht ziehen, um ähnliche Vorfälle in der Zukunft zu verhindern.
