Translate the text below into German. Keep names and identifiers unchanged. Return only the translation.
Text: Recent intelligence has highlighted a concerning trend within our network environment, indicative of opportunistic domain registrants engaging in malicious activities. These individuals or entities, motivated by a range of objectives, including financial gain or disruption, have been observed compromising private and enterprise networks through man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks across the Internet. These attacks are not isolated incidents but part of a broader pattern that has persisted over several months, affecting various geographical regions. The threat actors do not appear to leverage specific malware or exploit known vulnerabilities (CVEs), indicating a reliance on user behavior and network misconfigurations for their operations. The nature of these attacks suggests that they are opportunistic and adaptive, constantly evolving their tactics to circumvent defenses. Targets vary, ranging from small businesses to large enterprises, often based on identifying vulnerable points in the network infrastructure. The primary impact of these MitM attacks has been the interception of sensitive data during transmission. This can include login credentials, financial data, and other critical information that can be exploited by the attackers. Given the nature of these attacks, it is crucial that our security team remains vigilant and proactive in monitoring network traffic and implementing robust security protocols. Mitigations against these attacks are complex and multifaceted. While technical solutions such as encryption and secure authentication mechanisms are essential, regular security awareness training for employees and partners is equally important. Network segmentation and regular security audits can also help in reducing the attack surface and mitigating the potential impact. It is imperative that our team remains informed about emerging trends and best practices in cybersecurity to stay one step ahead of these opportunistic threat actors.
messages.output: Neue Intelligenz hat einen besorgniserregenden Trend in unserem Netzwerkumfeld hervorgehoben, der darauf hinweist, dass opportunistische Domänennutzer sich an böswilligen Tätigkeiten beteiligen. Diese Individuen oder Einheiten, motiviert durch eine Reihe von Zielen, einschließlich finanzieller Gewinnung oder Unterbrechung, haben beobachtete Versuche zur Verschlechterung privater und betrieblicher Netzwerke durch Man-in-the-Middle-Angriffe (MitM) im Internet. Diese Angriffe sind keine isolierten Vorfälle, sondern Teil eines breiteren Musters, das über mehrere Monate hinweg bestanden hat und verschiedene geografische Regionen betroffen hat. Die Betroffenen scheinen keine spezifischen Malware oder Exploits für bekannte Schwachstellen (CVEs) zu nutzen, was darauf hindeutet, dass sie ihre Operationen auf das Verhalten der Nutzer und Netzwerkkonfigurationen basieren. Die Natur dieser Angriffe deutet darauf hin, dass sie opportunistisch und adäptiv sind und ihre Taktiken ständig verändern, um Verteidigungen zu umgehen. Die Zielgruppen reichen von kleinen Unternehmen bis hin zu großen Unternehmen und basieren oft darauf, Schwachstellen in der Netzwerkinfrastruktur zu identifizieren. Der HauptEinfluss dieser MitM-Angriffe besteht darin, dass vertrauliche Daten während der Übertragung abgefangen werden. Dies kann darin bestehen, dass Login-Credentials, finanzielle Daten und andere kritische Informationen abgefangen werden, die von den Angreifern ausgenutzt werden können. Angesichts der Natur dieser Angriffe ist es entscheidend, dass unser Sicherheitsteam wachsam und proaktiv ist, um Netzwerkdurchfluss zu überwachen und umfassende Sicherheitsprotokolle einzuführen. Die Widerstandsmaßnahmen gegen diese Angriffe sind komplex und vielschichtig. Während technische Lösungen wie Verschlüsselung und sichere Authentifizierungsmechanismen essentiell sind, ist regelmäßige Sicherheitsbewusstseinsbildung für Mitarbeiter und Partner genauso wichtig. Netzwerkspezialisierung und regelmäßige Sicherheitsaudits können auch dazu beitragen, das Angriffsprofil zu reduzieren und den möglichen Einfluss zu mindern. Es ist entscheidend, dass unser Team sich über neu auftretende Trends und -praktiken in der Cyber-Sicherheit informiert, um einen Schritt voraus zu sein gegenüber diesen opportunistischen Bedrohungen.

Text: On September 20, 2016, and during the following weeks, our threat landscape was significantly impacted by a series of devastating distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks. The targets, KrebsOnSecurity.com and OVH, were hit with unprecedented intensity, causing their websites and services to be crippled for extended periods. These attacks were executed using two known malware variants: Mirai and Bashlite. Both of these malware strains are notorious for their ability to leverage default usernames and passwords to gain unauthorized access to IoT devices and other internet-connected systems. The initial attack on KrebsOnSecurity.com occurred on September 20, 2016, marking the beginning of a series of coordinated DDoS efforts. These attacks continued into late September and early October, with OVH experiencing its first major hit around early October. The attackers utilized a combination of Mirai and Bashlite to flood the targeted servers with traffic, overwhelming their capacity to handle legitimate user requests and causing significant downtime. The attackers leveraged the default usernames and passwords of compromised devices to gain control over a vast botnet, which they then used to launch these attacks. This method of attack is particularly concerning as it can affect a wide range of devices, from home routers to industrial control systems, potentially impacting multiple sectors and industries. The impact of these attacks was substantial, not only disrupting the availability of critical online resources but also highlighting the vulnerabilities in our current cybersecurity landscape. As we move forward, it is crucial that all stakeholders, from individual users to large enterprises, adopt robust security practices, including changing default credentials and implementing stronger security measures to mitigate the risk of such attacks.

These attacks were executed using two known malware variants: Mirai and Bashlite. Both of these malware strains are notorious for their ability to leverage default usernames and passwords to gain unauthorized access to IoT devices and other internet-connected systems. The initial attack on KrebsOnSecurity.com occurred on September 20, 2016, marking the beginning of a series of coordinated DDoS efforts. These attacks continued into late September and early October, with OVH experiencing its first major hit around early October. The attackers utilized a combination of Mirai and Bashlite to flood the targeted servers with traffic, overwhelming their capacity to handle legitimate user requests and causing significant downtime. The attackers leveraged the default usernames and passwords of compromised devices to gain control over a vast botnet, which they then used to launch these attacks. This method of attack is particularly concerning as it can affect a wide range of devices, from home routers to industrial control systems, potentially impacting multiple sectors and industries. The impact of these attacks was substantial, not only disrupting the availability of critical online resources but also highlighting the vulnerabilities in our current cybersecurity landscape. As we move forward, it is crucial that all stakeholders, from individual users to large enterprises, adopt robust security practices, including changing default credentials and implementing stronger security measures to mitigate the risk of such attacks.

September 2016 und in den folgenden Wochen wurde unser Bedrohungsszenario durch eine Reihe katastrophaler verteilter Leistungsabfälle (Distributed Denial of Service, DDoS-Angriffe) erheblich beeinflusst. Die Ziele, KrebsOnSecurity.com und OVH, wurden mit unvorhergesehener Intensität getroffen, was zur Verkuppelung ihrer Websites und Dienste führte. Diese Angriffe wurden mit zwei bekannten Malware-Variationen, namely Mirai und Bashlite, ausgeführt. Diese beiden Malware-Sträne sind berüchtigt dafür, dass sie die Fähigkeit haben, Standard Benutzernamen und Passwörter zu nutzen, um unberechtigten Zugriff auf IoT-Geräte und andere Internet-verbundene Systeme zu gewinnen. Der Angriff auf KrebsOnSecurity.com fand am 20. September 2016 statt, und das markierte den Beginn einer Reihe von koordinierten DDoS-Angriffen. Diese Angriffe setzten bis Ende September und Anfang Oktober fort, und OVH erlitt seine erste große Niederlage um Anfang Oktober. Die Angreifer nutzten eine Kombination aus Mirai und Bashlite, um den Ziel-Server mit Datenfluss zu überschwemmen, was ihre Fähigkeit, legitime Nutzeranfragen zu bearbeiten, überwältigte und zu einer signifikanten Downtime führte. Die Angreifer nutzten die Standard Benutzernamen und Passwörter der vercompromittierten Geräte, um Kontrolle über ein umfangreiches Botnetz zu gewinnen, das sie dann zum Ausführen dieser Angriffe nutzten. Diese Art des Angriffs ist besorgniserregend, da sie eine Vielzahl von Geräten, von Heimrouter bis zu industriellen Steuerungssystemen, betreffen kann, potenziell mehrere Sektoren und Branchen auswirken kann. Der Einfluss dieser Angriffe war erheblich, nicht nur indem sie die Verfügbarkeit kritischer online-Ressourcen störten, sondern auch indem sie die Schwachstellen in unserer aktuellen Cyber-Sicherheitslandschaft hervorhoben. In der Zukunft ist es wichtig, dass alle Stakeholder, von Einzelnen bis hin zu großen Unternehmen, robuste Sicherheitspraktiken anwenden, einschließlich Änderung der Standardbenutzerkonten und Einsetzen stärkerer Sicherheitsmaßnahmen, um den Risiko solcher Angriffe zu mindern.

Example 1: This Malware Analysis Report (MAR) is the result of analytic efforts by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to provide detailed analysis of files associated with HyperBro, a Remote Access Trojan (RAT). CISA obtained HyperBro malware samples during an on-site incident response engagement at a Defense Industrial Base (DIB) Sector organization compromised by advanced persistent threat (APT) actors. CISA analyzed 4 files associated with HyperBro malware. The files creates a backdoor program that is capable of uploading and downloading files to and from the system. The RAT is also capable of logging keystrokes and executing commands on the system. For more information on the confirmed compromise, see Joint CSA: Impacket and Exfiltration Tool Used to Steal Sensitive Information from Defense Industrial Base Organization . This artifact is a version of vf_host.exe from Viewfinity. The file is used to side-load the malicious dynamic-link library (DLL), vftrace.dll. The program is also capable of bypassing User Account Controls (UAC) on the system by disabling Admin Approval Mode in User Account Controls Group Policy in HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System. This can allow the malware to run with Admin privileges, or allow remote logon (RDP) with full Admin privileges.

Example 2: As organizations adapt or change their enterprise collaboration capabilities to meet "telework" requirements, many organizations are migrating to Microsoft Office 365 (O365) and other cloud collaboration services. Due to the speed of these deployments, organizations may not be fully considering the security configurations of these platforms. This Alert is an update to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's May 2019 Analysis Report, AR19-133A: Microsoft Office 365 Security Observations , and reiterates the recommendations related to O365 for organizations to review and ensure their newly adopted environment is configured to protect, detect, and respond against would be attackers of O365. Since October 2018, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has conducted several engagements with customers who have migrated to cloud-based collaboration solutions like O365. In recent weeks, organizations have been forced to change their collaboration methods to support a full "work from home" workforce. O365 provides cloud-based email capabilities, as well as chat and video capabilities using Microsoft Teams. While the abrupt shift to work-from-home may necessitate rapid deployment of cloud collaboration services, such as O365, hasty deployment can lead to oversights in security configurations and undermine a sound O365-specific security strategy. CISA continues to see instances where entities are not implementing best security practices in regard to their O365 implementation, resulting in increased vulnerability to adversary attacks.

This Cybersecurity Advisory is based on observations and analysis conducted by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) following a series of significant distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks against targeted organizations. The attacks, which began on September 20, 2016, and continued into late September and early October, were attributed to the use of Mirai and Bashlite, two variants of the same malware family. The targets of these attacks included Krebs on Security, a well-known cybersecurity blog, and OVH, a major European web hosting and cloud services provider, both of which experienced crippling DDoS attacks that significantly impacted their services.

Mirai and Bashlite, both known for leveraging default usernames and passwords, were employed to create a botnet that launched these attacks. The malware variants exploited known vulnerabilities in IoT devices, network cameras, and other internet-connected devices, often with default credentials, to gain access and control over these devices. By doing so, attackers were able to recruit a large number of devices into their botnet, significantly amplifying the impact of each DDoS attack.

The impact of these attacks was substantial, leading to service outages and operational disruptions for the affected organizations. Krebs on Security reported experiencing a 620 Gbps DDoS attack, one of the largest recorded at the time. Similarly, OVH faced a 1 Tbps DDoS attack, which disrupted their services for a considerable period. These attacks highlighted the vulnerabilities associated with default credentials and the importance of strong security practices, particularly in the context of IoT devices and internet-connected infrastructure.

While CISA did not identify any specific TTPs or CVEs related to these attacks, the advisory serves as a reminder of the risks associated with default credentials and the need for organizations to implement robust security measures, including regular password updates and device hardening, to mitigate the threat of such attacks.

The attackers employed a combination of phishing emails and money mule schemes to infiltrate these institutions. The malware involved includes various variants, with a notable presence of Avalanche-associated malware, which was used to steal sensitive personal information, launch Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks, and distribute additional malware. The attackers also stole user credentials and made ransom demands, further exacerbating the impact. Indicators of compromise included the use of fast-flux DNS, allowing the attackers to rapidly change the IP addresses associated with their command and control servers, complicating detection and response efforts. The financial sector was the primary target, with the attacks spanning multiple institutions. The comprehensive nature of the threat, involving multiple attack techniques and vectors, underscores the need for robust and vigilant security measures to prevent such incidents.

Microsoft will continue to provide free security updates to those systems through the 2020 election. See Microsoft's article, Extending free Windows 7 security updates to voting systems , for more information. On January 14, 2020, Microsoft will end extended support for their Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2 operating systems. After this date, these products will no longer receive free technical support, or software and security updates. Organizations that have regulatory obligations may find that they are unable to satisfy compliance requirements while running Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2. All software products have a lifecycle. "End of support" refers to the date when the software vendor will no longer provide automatic fixes, updates, or online technical assistance. Systems running Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2 will continue to work at their current capacity even after support ends on January 14, 2020. However, using unsupported software may increase the likelihood of malware and other security threats. Mission and business functions supported by systems running Windows 7 and Windows Server 2008 R2 could experience negative consequences resulting from unpatched vulnerabilities and software bugs. These negative consequences could include the loss of confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data, system resources, and business assets.

Example 2: After initial access, the threat actor performed Discovery [ TA0007 ] by logging into an agency O365 email account from and viewing and downloading help desk email attachments with "Intranet access" and "VPN passwords" in the subject line, despite already having privileged access (Email Collection [ T1114 ], Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files [ T1552.001 ]). (Note: these emails did not contain any passwords.) The actor logged into the same email account via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) from IP address ( External Remote Services [ T1133 ]). The actor enumerated the Active Directory and Group Policy key and changed a registry key for the Group Policy ( Account Manipulation [ T1098 ]). Immediately afterward, the threat actor used common Microsoft Windows command line processes- , , , , , , and , -to enumerate the compromised system and network ( Command and Scripting Interpreter [ T1059 ], System Network Configuration Discovery [ T1016 ]). The cyber threat actor then attempted multiple times to connect to virtual private server (VPS) IP through a Windows Server Message Block (SMB) client. Although they connected and disconnected multiple times, the connections were ultimately successful. During the same period, the actor used an alias secure identifier account they had previously created to log into VPS via an SMB share. The attacker then executed on a victim file server ( Command and Scripting Interpreter [ T1059 ]). ( is a command-line version of PuTTy that is used for remote administration.) Text: This internal threat bulletin highlights the recent activities of an unknown actor who has employed a sophisticated, multi-pronged approach to compromise our network. The threat actors have leveraged both PLUGX/SOGU and REDLEAVES malware, known for their advanced capabilities, including the use of PowerShell and PowerSploit scripts, which allow for the execution of commands and scripts with elevated privileges, providing a persistent foothold in the network. Additionally, RC4 cipher communications over port 443 are used to obfuscate their activities and maintain stealth, making it challenging to detect and mitigate their presence. The primary objective of this intrusion appears to be user impersonation via compromised credentials, with the threat actors planting malware implants on key relay and staging machines. This approach ensures that once the initial compromise is achieved, the threat actors can maintain control over the network and exfiltrate sensitive information at their leisure. The use of DLL side-loading further complicates the detection of these implants, as it allows for the execution of malicious code without altering the system's main executable files. To identify and mitigate these threats, our security team is advised to implement the following mitigations: Monitor for potential malicious activity on your network, paying close attention to anomalies in network traffic, unusual PowerShell script execution, and unexpected connections on port 443. Use the provided indicators of compromise, which include domains, IP addresses, and dynamic DNS services, to observe potential malicious activity. Regularly updating these lists will help in identifying and isolating compromised systems. Employ anti-virus signatures to detect the presence of PLUGX/SOGU and REDLEAVES malware, ensuring that any detected threats are promptly addressed and removed to prevent further damage. By implementing these strategies, we can enhance our defenses against these sophisticated threats and reduce the risk of a successful compromise.

Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: Note: critical infrastructure organizations with industrial control systems/operational technology networks should review joint CISA-FBI Cybersecurity Advisory AA21-131A: DarkSide Ransomware: Best Practices for Preventing Business Disruption from Ransomware Attacks for more mitigations, including mitigations to reduce the risk of severe business or functional degradation should their entity fall victim to a ransomware attack. Note: CISA, the FBI, and NSA strongly discourage paying a ransom to criminal actors. Paying a ransom may embolden adversaries to target additional organizations, encourage other criminal actors to engage in the distribution of ransomware, and/or may fund illicit activities. Paying the ransom also does not guarantee that a victim's files will be recovered. This document was developed by CISA, the FBI, and NSA in furtherance of their respective cybersecurity missions, including their responsibilities to develop and issue cybersecurity specifications and mitigations. Note: the information you have accessed is being provided "as is" for informational purposes only. CISA, the FBI, and NSA do not endorse any commercial product or service, including any subjects of analysis. Any reference to specific commercial products, processes, or services by service mark, trademark, manufacturer, or otherwise, does not constitute or imply their endorsement, recommendation, or favoring by CISA, the FBI, or NSA.

Example 2: In one case, CISA determined that the threat actors modified an existing email rule on a user's account-originally set by the user to forward emails sent from a certain sender to a personal account-to redirect the emails to an account controlled by the actors. The threat actors updated the rule to forward all email to the threat actors' accounts. Threat actors also modified existing rules to search users' email messages (subject and body) for several finance-related keywords (which contained spelling mistakes) and forward the emails to the threat actors' account. In addition to modifying existing user email rules, the threat actors created new mailbox rules that forwarded certain messages received by the users (specifically, messages with certain phishing-related keywords) to the legitimate users' Really Simple Syndication (RSS) Feeds or RSS Subscriptions folder in an effort to prevent warnings from being seen by the legitimate users. CISA verified that the threat actors successfully signed into one user's account with proper multi-factor authentication (MFA). In this case, CISA believes the threat actors may have used browser cookies to defeat MFA with a "pass-the-cookie" attack ( Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie [ T1550.004 ]). The threat actors attempted brute force logins ( Brute Force [ T1110 ]) on some accounts. However, this activity was not successful. This thwarted attempt was due, in part, to the threat actors not guessing a correct username/password combination, as well as the organization's use of MFA to access their cloud environment. This Analysis Report uses the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK®) framework. See the ATT&CK for Enterprise framework for all referenced threat actor tactics and techniques.

Die Bedrohungsmuster haben sowohl das PLUGX/SOGU- als auch das REDLEAVES-Malware-Tool genutzt, die für ihre fortgeschrittenen Fähigkeiten bekannt sind, einschließlich dem Verwenden von PowerShell- und PowerSploit-Skripten, die es ihnen ermöglichen, Befehle und Skripte mit erhöhten Rechten auszuführen, was einen beständigen Zugang im Netzwerk gewährleistet. Darüber hinaus nutzen sie Verschlüsselungen mit dem RC4-Verschlüsselungsalgorithmus über Port 443, um ihre Aktivitäten zu verbergen und ihren Hintergrund zu vertuschen, was das Erkennen und Bekämpfen ihres Vorhandenseins schwierig macht. Der primäre Zielpunkt dieser Eindringen scheint die Benutzeridentifikation über kompromittiertere Zugangsdaten zu sein, während die Bedrohungsmuster Malware-Implantsate auf Schlüsselrelay- und -Stagingmaschinen platzieren. Dieser Ansatz gewährleistet, dass sie, sobald die initiale Kompromittierung erreicht ist, über Kontrolle über das Netzwerk verfügen und vertrauliche Informationen in ihrer Freizeit extrahieren können. Das Verwenden von DLL-Sideloading verstärkt weiterhin das Erkennen dieser Implantaaten, da es das Ausführen von schädlichem Code ohne Änderung der Hauptexecutable-Dateien des Systems ermöglicht. Um diese Bedrohungen zu identifizieren und zu bekämpfen, wird der Sicherheitsstab empfohlen, die folgenden Maßnahmen einzuführen: Beobachten Sie mögliche schädliche Aktivitäten im Netzwerk und achten Sie besonders auf Auffälligkeiten im Netzwerkbetrieb, ungewöhnliche PowerShell-Skriptausführungen und unerwartete Verbindungen über Port 443. Nutzen Sie die bereitgestellten Indikatoren der bekannten Bedrohungen, die Domänen, IP-Adressen und dynamische DNS-Dienste um, um mögliche schädliche Aktivitäten zu beobachten. Die regelmäßige Aktualisierung dieser Listen hilft, verkompromittierte Systeme zu identifizieren und zu isolieren. Nutzen Sie Anti-Virus-Signaturen, um die Anwesenheit von PLUGX/SOGU- und REDLEAVES-Malware zu erkennen, und stellen Sie sicher, dass bei der Erkennung von Bedrohungen die betroffenen Bedrohungen umgehend angepasst und entfernt werden, um eine weitere Schadensausbreitung zu vermeiden. Text: This internal threat bulletin highlights a significant security incident characterized by unauthorized access to network devices within our organization. The unauthorized access, which has been confirmed, poses a direct threat to the integrity and confidentiality of our network infrastructure. The intrusion appears to be the result of a sophisticated attack, likely executed by a well-resourced and knowledgeable adversary. While specific malware or known vulnerabilities (CVEs) were not identified, the breach may have been achieved through social engineering or exploitation of default configurations. To mitigate this risk, it is imperative that all network devices are secured with the latest firmware updates and that SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is deployed using SNMPv3, the secure version of the protocol. Additionally, implementing MIB (Management Information Base) whitelisting can significantly reduce the risk of unauthorized access by restricting the types of MIB objects that can be accessed. Furthermore, ensuring that all network devices are configured securely, with minimal exposure to external networks, is crucial. By adhering to these recommendations, we can bolster our defenses against unauthorized access and maintain the security and confidentiality of our network devices.

Der unbefugte Zugang, dessen Vorliegen bestätigt wurde, stellt eine direkte Bedrohung für die Integrität und Konfidentialität unseres Netzwerks dar. Die Eindringlichkeit scheint das Ergebnis eines anspruchsvollen Angriffs zu sein, der höchstwahrscheinlich von einer gut ausgerüsteten und wissenden Gegenseite durchgeführt wurde. Ob spezifische Malware oder bekannte Schwachstellen (CVEs) identifiziert wurden, konnte nicht nachgewiesen werden, die Verletzung könnte jedoch durch Sozial engineering oder Ausnutzung der Standardkonfigurationen erreicht worden sein. Um diesen Risikofaktor zu minimieren, ist es unerlässlich, dass alle Netzwerkkonfigurationen mit der neuesten Firmware aktualisiert sind und SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) mit SNMPv3, der sicheren Version des Protokolls, eingesetzt wird. Zudem kann die Implementierung einer MIB-Whitelisting den Risikofaktor unbefugten Zugangs erheblich reduzieren, indem sie den Zugriff auf bestimmte MIB-Objekte einschränkt. Zusätzlich ist die sichere Konfiguration aller Netzwerkkonfigurationen, mit minimaler Exposition gegenüber externen Netzwerken, entscheidend. Indem wir diese Empfehlungen einhalten, können wir unsere Abwehrkräfte gegen unbefugten Zugang stärken und die Sicherheit und Konfidentialität unserer Netzwerkkonfigurationen sichern.

### Unauthorized Access to Network Devices

Analysts should be vigilant for unauthorized access to network devices, which can have severe implications for the integrity and security of the network. This advisory highlights the importance of implementing robust mitigations to prevent such incidents. The primary method of unauthorized access often involves exploiting weak authentication mechanisms, particularly Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) services.

To mitigate these risks, it is recommended to implement the following measures:

1. **Use SNMPv3**: Upgrade from SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c to SNMPv3, which provides enhanced security through encrypted authentication and privacy.
   
2. **Combine with MIB Whitelisting**: Implement MIB whitelisting to restrict access to only those Management Information Base (MIB) objects that are essential for network monitoring and management. This limits the potential for unauthorized access by reducing the attack surface.
   
3. **Use Secure Configurations**: Ensure that network devices are configured securely, including disabling unnecessary services and protocols, and applying the principle of least privilege to all device configurations.

Additional indicators of unauthorized access may include unusual login attempts, unauthorized configuration changes, or unexpected traffic patterns. Analysts should review log entries related to SNMP for any suspicious activity, such as repeated authentication failures or attempts to access non-standard MIB objects.

For a live system, analysts can use the following command to check for unauthorized changes:
```shell
snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u <username> -a SHA -A <password> -x AES -X <priv-password> <ip-address> <oid>
```
This command should be executed with caution to avoid false positives and ensure accurate results.

In cases where unauthorized access has occurred, it is crucial to conduct a thorough investigation and consider the following actions:
- **Review device logs** for any unauthorized access attempts.
- **Monitor network traffic** for signs of data exfiltration or other malicious activities.
- **Update and patch all devices** to ensure they are protected against known vulnerabilities.

By adhering to these recommendations, organizations can significantly reduce the risk of unauthorized access and enhance the overall security posture of their network infrastructure.

Timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats. On January 14, 2020, Microsoft released software fixes to address 49 vulnerabilities as part of their monthly Patch Tuesday announcement. Among the vulnerabilities patched were critical weaknesses in Windows CryptoAPI, Windows Remote Desktop Gateway (RD Gateway), and Windows Remote Desktop Client. An attacker could remotely exploit these vulnerabilities to decrypt, modify, or inject data on user connections: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is unaware of active exploitation of these vulnerabilities. However, because patches have been publicly released, the underlying vulnerabilities can be reverse-engineered to create exploits that target unpatched systems. CISA strongly recommends organizations install these critical patches as soon as possible-prioritize patching by starting with mission critical systems, internet-facing systems, and networked servers. Organizations should then prioritize patching other affected information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) assets. According to Microsoft, "an attacker could exploit the vulnerability by using a spoofed code-signing certificate to sign a malicious executable, making it appear the file was from a trusted, legitimate source. The user would have no way of knowing the file was malicious, because the digital signature would appear to be from a trusted provider." Additionally, "a successful exploit could also allow the attacker to conduct man-in-the-middle attacks and decrypt confidential information on user connections to the affected software." A cyber attacker could exploit CVE-2020-0601 to obtain sensitive information, such as financial information, or run malware on a targeted system; for example: The National Security Agency (NSA) provides detection measures for CVE-2020-0601 in their Cybersecurity Advisory: Patch Critical Cryptographic Vulnerability in Microsoft Windows Clients and Servers . Microsoft's security update for the MS17-010 SMB vulnerability is highly recommended to mitigate the risk of exploitation. Organizations should prioritize patching their systems, starting with mission critical servers and internet-facing assets, to reduce the likelihood of infection.

Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: The cyber actor used SoftPerfect Network Scanner for Discovery [ TA0007 ] of hostnames and network services ( Network Service Scanning [ T1046 ]). The artifact is a stand-alone version of the SoftPerfect Network Scanner, version 7.2.9 for 64-bit operating systems. The SoftPerfect website states that the "SoftPerfect Network Scanner can ping computers, scan ports, discover shared folders, and retrieve practically any information about network devices, via Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI), Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP), Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), Secure Shell (SSH), and PowerShell. It also scans for remote services, registry, files and performance counters; offers flexible filtering and display options and exports NetScan results to a variety of formats from XML to JSON." The utility can also be used with Nmap for vulnerability scanning. The utility will generate a report of its findings called . The artifact is an Extensible Markup Language (XML) document reporting scanning results for the SoftPerfect Network Scanner program. The XML document indicates that a random scan was conducted to identify hostnames on a network and to search for: A license is required to unlock all of the features of the SoftPerfect Network Scanner. The artifact is the Network Scanner license that was included with this submission. The license name is . The malicious cyber actor used PsExec to execute , which CISA refers to as FiveHands ransomware ( Execution [ TA0002 ], System Services: Service Execution [ T1569.002 ], Impact [ TA0040 ]). FiveHands is a novel ransomware variant that uses a public key encryption scheme called . Note: the NTRUEncrypt public key cryptosystem encryption algorithm (NTRU), is a lattice-based alternative to Rivest-Shamir-Adleman, known as RSA, and Elliptic-curve cryptography, or ECC, and is based on the shortest vector problem in a lattice.

Example 2: Securing end-to-end communications plays an important role in protecting privacy and preventing some forms of man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks. Recently, researchers described a MITM attack used to inject code, causing unsecured web browsers around the world to become unwitting participants in a distributed denial-of-service attack. That same code can be employed to deliver an exploit for a particular vulnerability or to take other arbitrary actions. A MITM attack occurs when a third party inserts itself between the communications of a client and a server. MITM attacks as a general class are not new. Classic MITM attacks (e.g., ARP Spoofing) focus on redirecting network communications. By definition, network infrastructure under attacker control is vulnerable to MITM. However, as technology evolves, new methods for performing MITM attacks evolve as well. Currently, there is no single technology or configuration to prevent all MITM attacks. However, increasing the complexity with multiple layers of defense may raise the cost for the attacker. Increasing the attacker's cost in time, effort, or money can be an effective deterrent to avoiding future network compromise. Generally, encryption and digital certificates provide an effective safeguard against MITM attacks, assuring both the confidentiality and integrity of communications. As a result, modern MITM attacks have focused on taking advantage of weaknesses in the cryptographic infrastructure (e.g., certificate authorities (CAs), web browser certificate stores) or the encryption algorithms and protocols themselves. MITM attacks are critical because of the wide range of potential impacts-these include the exposure of sensitive information, modification of trusted data, and injection of data. Employing multiple network and browser protection methods forces an attacker to develop different tactics, techniques, and procedures to circumvent the new security configuration.

messages.output:
The cyber actor NotPetya, in an elaborate attack, leveraged a modified version of the Mimikatz tool to steal Windows credentials [T1003], indicating a sophisticated understanding of internal network security measures. This technique allowed the actor to exploit trust relationships within the target environment, ensuring deeper penetration and broader access. Concurrently, NotPetya utilized the EternalBlue exploit tool, targeting unpatched systems running a vulnerable version of SMBv1 [T1566.007]. The EternalBlue exploit, initially developed for the exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability in the Server Message Block version 1 (SMBv1) protocol, was re-purposed by the actor for malicious intent, spreading rapidly across networks. NotPetya’s campaign began with a backdoor compromise on April 14, 2017, setting the stage for further exploitation. The primary delivery mechanism materialized on June 27, 2017, when systems were unwittingly infected, marking the start of the widespread damage. The malware utilized the `psexec.exe` utility [TA0002] to initiate the ransomware payload, leveraging its ability to execute processes on a remote system as a means of persistence and rapid spread.

Upon successful execution, NotPetya encrypted files on infected systems using a 128-bit AES algorithm, rendering them inaccessible and potentially irreparable [TA0033]. The impact of this action was significant, affecting critical business operations and leading to substantial financial losses for affected organizations. Organizations were advised to treat systems with M.E.Doc installed, a Ukrainian accounting software, as suspicious, as its presence may indicate a targeted attack vector. Additionally, the incident highlighted the importance of examining systems for additional malicious activity, as NotPetya often acted in conjunction with other forms of cyber threats to maximize its impact.

Mitigation strategies include patching systems running a vulnerable version of SMBv1 to prevent the EternalBlue exploit from being effective [TA0012]. Organizations should also implement strict monitoring and anomaly detection systems to identify and respond to suspicious activity in a timely manner. By treating systems with M.E.Doc as potentially compromised, organizations can isolate and secure these systems, minimizing the spread of the malware. Overall, the NotPetya attack underscores the need for robust security practices, continuous system updates, and thorough monitoring to safeguard against sophisticated and widespread cyber threats.

For more information see the Microsoft Knowledge Base article, KB5014754-Certificate-based authentication changes on Windows domain controllers: Key Distribution Center registry key . Note: installation of updates released May 10, 2022, on client Windows devices and non-domain controller Windows Servers will not cause this issue and is still strongly encouraged. Example 2: On July 13, 2020 EST, SAP released a security update to address a critical vulnerability, CVE-2020-6287, affecting the SAP NetWeaver Application Server (AS) Java component LM Configuration Wizard. An unauthenticated attacker can exploit this vulnerability through the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) to take control of trusted SAP applications. Due to the criticality of this vulnerability, the attack surface this vulnerability represents, and the importance of SAP's business applications, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) strongly recommends organizations immediately apply patches. CISA recommends organizations prioritize patching internet-facing systems, and then internal systems. Organizations that are unable to immediately patch should mitigate the vulnerability by disabling the LM Configuration Wizard service (see SAP Security Note #2939665 ). Should these options be unavailable or if the actions will take more than 24 hours to complete, CISA strongly recommends closely monitoring your SAP NetWeaver AS for anomalous activity. CISA is unaware of any active exploitation of these vulnerabilities at the time of this report. However, because patches have been publicly released, the underlying vulnerabilities could be reverse-engineered to create exploits that target unpatched systems. This vulnerability is present by default in SAP applications running on top of SAP NetWeaver AS Java 7.3 and any newer versions (up to SAP NetWeaver 7.5). Potentially vulnerable SAP business solutions include any SAP Java-based solutions such as (but not limited to): The vulnerability was identified in a component that is part of the SAP NetWeaver AS Java. This technology stack is part of the SAP Solution Manager, which is a support and system management suite. The SAP NetWeaver AS for Java technology supports the SAP Portal component, which may therefore be affected by this vulnerability and is typically exposed to the internet. Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: A number of actors have used COVID-19-related phishing to steal user credentials. These emails include previously mentioned COVID-19 social engineering techniques, sometimes complemented with urgent language to enhance the lure. If the user clicks on the hyperlink, a spoofed login webpage appears that includes a password entry form. These spoofed login pages may relate to a wide array of online services including-but not limited to-email services provided by Google or Microsoft, or services accessed via government websites. To further entice the recipient, the websites will often contain COVID-19-related wording within the URL (e.g., "corona-virus-business-update," "covid19-advisory," or "cov19esupport"). These spoofed pages are designed to look legitimate or accurately impersonate well-known websites. Often the only way to notice malicious intent is through examining the website URL. In some circumstances, malicious cyber actors specifically customize these spoofed login webpages for the intended victim. If the victim enters their password on the spoofed page, the attackers will be able to access the victim's online accounts, such as their email inbox. This access can then be used to acquire personal or sensitive information, or to further disseminate phishing emails, using the victim's address book. A number of threat actors have used COVID-19-related lures to deploy malware. In most cases, actors craft an email that persuades the victim to open an attachment or download a malicious file from a linked website. When the victim opens the attachment, the malware is executed, compromising the victim's device. For example, NCSC has observed various email messages that deploy the "Agent Tesla" keylogger malware. The email appears to be sent from Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO. This email campaign began on Thursday, March 19, 2020. Another similar campaign offers thermometers and face masks to fight the epidemic. The email purports to attach images of these medical products but instead contains a loader for Agent Tesla.

Example 2: This joint Cybersecurity Advisory uses the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK®) framework, Version 9. See the ATT&CK for Enterprise framework for referenced threat actor techniques and for mitigations. This joint advisory is the result of analytic efforts between the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) to highlight the cyber threat associated with active exploitation of a newly identified vulnerability (CVE-2021-44077) in Zoho ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus-IT help desk software with asset management. CVE-2021-44077, which Zoho rated critical, is an unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability affecting all ServiceDesk Plus versions up to, and including, version 11305. This vulnerability was addressed by the update released by Zoho on September 16, 2021 for ServiceDesk Plus versions 11306 and above. The FBI and CISA assess that advanced persistent threat (APT) cyber actors are among those exploiting the vulnerability. Successful exploitation of the vulnerability allows an attacker to upload executable files and place webshells, which enable the adversary to conduct post-exploitation activities, such as compromising administrator credentials, conducting lateral movement, and exfiltrating registry hives and Active Directory files. The Zoho update that patched this vulnerability was released on September 16, 2021, along with a security advisory . Additionally, an email advisory was sent to all ServiceDesk Plus customers with additional information. Zoho released a subsequent security advisory on November 22, 2021 , and advised customers to patch immediately. The FBI and CISA are aware of reports of malicious cyber actors likely using exploits against CVE-2021-44077 to gain access [ T1190 ] to ManageEngine ServiceDesk Plus, as early as late October 2021. The actors have been observed using various tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs), including: Sharing technical and/or qualitative information with the FBI and CISA helps empower and amplify our capabilities as federal partners to collect and share intelligence and engage with victims, while working to unmask and hold accountable those conducting malicious cyber activities.

Threat actors have been exploiting web application vulnerabilities or configuration weaknesses to install web shells, which provide a backdoor for remote access. Specifically, the actors have been targeting the admin interface, which often includes a file upload option-a critical security flaw that can be leveraged to inject malicious code. The exploitation methods are varied and sophisticated, potentially indicating a well-coordinated and resourceful threat actor. The presence of these web shells represents a significant risk as they can be used to exfiltrate sensitive data, install additional malware, or maintain persistent access. Our analysis indicates that these vulnerabilities are likely due to outdated software, unpatched systems, or misconfigurations that allow attackers to upload and execute scripts. The impact of such an intrusion could range from data breaches to complete system compromise. To mitigate these threats, we recommend a proactive approach. First, all web applications must undergo a thorough security assessment to identify and close any existing vulnerabilities. This includes both software vulnerabilities and configuration weaknesses that could be exploited. Additionally, we should monitor and delete any suspicious or malicious files that have been uploaded through the admin interface. Many DPRK cyber actors are subordinate to UN- and U.S.-designated entities, such as the Reconnaissance General Bureau. DPRK state-sponsored cyber actors primarily consist of hackers, cryptologists, and software developers who conduct espionage, cyber-enabled theft targeting financial institutions and digital currency exchanges, and politically-motivated operations against foreign media companies. They develop and deploy a wide range of malware tools around the world to enable these activities and have grown increasingly sophisticated. Common tactics to raise revenue illicitly by DPRK state-sponsored cyber actors include, but are not limited to: Cyber-Enabled Financial Theft and Money Laundering. The UN Security Council 1718 Committee Panel of Experts' 2019 mid-term report (2019 POE mid-term report) states that the DPRK is increasingly able to generate revenue notwithstanding UN Security Council sanctions by using malicious cyber activities to steal from financial institutions through increasingly sophisticated tools and tactics. The 2019 POE mid-term report notes that, in some cases, these malicious cyber activities have also extended to laundering funds through multiple jurisdictions. The 2019 POE mid-term report mentions that it was investigating dozens of suspected DPRK cyber-enabled heists and that, as of late 2019, the DPRK has attempted to steal as much as $2 billion through these illicit cyber activities. Allegations in a March 2020 Department of Justice forfeiture complaint are consistent with portions of the POE's findings. Specifically, the forfeiture complaint alleged how North Korean cyber actors used North Korean infrastructure in furtherance of their conspiracy to hack digital currency exchanges, steal hundreds of millions of dollars in digital currency, and launder the funds.

Example 2: The National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center (NCCIC) is aware of ongoing APT actor activity attempting to infiltrate the networks of global managed service providers (MSPs). Since May 2016, APT actors have used various tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) for the purposes of cyber espionage and intellectual property theft. APT actors have targeted victims in several U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, including Information Technology (IT), Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Communications, and Critical Manufacturing. This Technical Alert (TA) provides information and guidance to assist MSP customer network and system administrators with the detection of malicious activity on their networks and systems and the mitigation of associated risks. This TA includes an overview of TTPs used by APT actors in MSP network environments, recommended mitigation techniques, and information on reporting incidents. MSPs provide remote management of customer IT and end-user systems. The number of organizations using MSPs has grown significantly over recent years because MSPs allow their customers to scale and support their network environments at a lower cost than financing these resources internally. MSPs generally have direct and unfettered access to their customers' networks, and may store customer data on their own internal infrastructure. By servicing a large number of customers, MSPs can achieve significant economies of scale. However, a compromise in one part of an MSP's network can spread globally, affecting other customers and introducing risk. Using an MSP significantly increases an organization's virtual enterprise infrastructure footprint and its number of privileged accounts, creating a larger attack surface for cyber criminals and nation-state actors. By using compromised legitimate MSP credentials (e.g., administration, domain, user), APT actors can move bidirectionally between an MSP and its customers' shared networks. Bidirectional movement between networks allows APT actors to easily obfuscate detection measures and maintain a presence on victims' networks. Note: NCCIC previously released information related to this activity in Alert TA17-117A: Intrusions Affecting Multiple Victims Across Multiple Sectors published on April 27, 2017, which includes indicators of compromise, signatures, suggested detection methods, and recommended mitigation techniques.

Text: In the past few weeks, our Security Operations Center (SOC) has observed a concerning trend within our network that warrants immediate attention. Threat actors have been exploiting web application vulnerabilities or configuration weaknesses to install web shells, which provide a backdoor for remote access. Specifically, the actors have been targeting the admin interface, which often includes a file upload option-a critical security flaw that can be leveraged to inject malicious code. The exploitation methods are varied and sophisticated, potentially indicating a well-coordinated and resourceful threat actor. The presence of these web shells represents a significant risk as they can be used to exfiltrate sensitive data, install additional malware, or maintain persistent access. Our analysis indicates that these vulnerabilities are likely due to outdated software, unpatched systems, or misconfigurations that allow attackers to upload and execute scripts. The impact of such an intrusion could range from data breaches to complete system compromise. To mitigate these threats, we recommend a proactive approach. First, all web applications must undergo a thorough security assessment to identify and close any existing vulnerabilities. This includes both software vulnerabilities and configuration weaknesses that could be exploited. Additionally, we should monitor and delete any suspicious or malicious files that have been uploaded through the admin interface. Regular security audits and adherence to best practices for web application security are crucial to preventing future incidents. By taking these steps, we can significantly reduce the risk of compromise and ensure the continued security and integrity of our systems. The importance of proactive security measures cannot be overstated, and we must remain vigilant in our efforts to protect our networks.
messages.output: In den letzten Wochen hat unser Security Operations Center (SOC) eine besorgniserregende Tendenz in unserem Netzwerk festgestellt, die sofortige Aufmerksamkeit erfordert. Drohnenakteure ausnutzen Webanwendungsfehler oder Konfigurationsmängel, um Web-Shells zu installieren, die eine Rückgängigmachung für den entfernten Zugriff bieten. Insbesondere haben die Akteure das Admin-Interface als Ziel gewählt, das häufig eine Dateiupload-Funktion beinhaltet – ein kritischer Sicherheitsloch, das dazu dienen kann, böswilliges Code einfließen zu lassen. Die Ausnutzungsmethoden sind vielseitig und verfeinert, was darauf hindeutet, dass es sich um ein gut koordiniertes und ressourcenreichen Drohnenaktor handelt. Die Anwesenheit dieser Web-Shells repräsentiert einen signifikanten Risikofaktor, da sie sensibles Daten exfiltrieren, zusätzliche Malware installieren oder einen fortbestehenden Zugriff gewährleisten können. Unsere Analyse zeigt an, dass diese Verwundbarkeiten wahrscheinlich auf veraltete Software, unpatchete Systeme oder Konfigurationen zurückzuführen sind, die Angreifer ermöglichen, Skripte hochzuladen und auszuführen. Die Auswirkungen einer solchen Eindringlichkeit könnten vom Datenverlust bis zur vollständigen Systemverwüstung reichen. Um diese Bedrohungen zu reduzieren, empfehlen wir eine vorbildliche Vorgehensweise. Zunächst müssen alle Webanwendungen gründlich Sicherheitsbewertungen unterworfen werden, um bestehende Verwundbarkeiten zu identifizieren und zu schließen. Dies umfasst sowohl Softwareverwundbarkeiten als auch Konfigurationsmängel, die ausgenutzt werden können. Darüber hinaus sollten wir überwachen und löschen, wenn möglich, verdächtige oder böswillige Dateien, die durch das Admin-Interface hochgeladen wurden. Regelmäßige Sicherheitsprüfungen und der Einhaltung bestehender Praktiken für die Sicherheit von Webanwendungen sind entscheidend, um zukünftige Inciden zu verhindern. Indem wir diese Schritte einleiten, können wir den Risikofaktor einer Eindringlichkeit signifikant reduzieren und die fortlaufende Sicherheit und Integrität unseres Systems gewährleisten. Die Bedeutung vorbildlicher Sicherheitsmaßnahmen kann nicht unterstrichen werden, und wir müssen in unseren Bemühungen, unsere Netzwerke zu schützen, stets wachsam bleiben.

Example 1: CISA, ACSC, the NCSC, and FBI assess that public and private organizations worldwide remain vulnerable to compromise from the exploitation of these CVEs. Malicious cyber actors will most likely continue to use older known vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2017-11882 affecting Microsoft Office, as long as they remain effective and systems remain unpatched. Adversaries' use of known vulnerabilities complicates attribution, reduces costs, and minimizes risk because they are not investing in developing a zero-day exploit for their exclusive use, which they risk losing if it becomes known. CISA, ACSC, the NCSC, and FBI have identified the following as the topmost exploited vulnerabilities by malicious cyber actors from 2020: CVE-2019-19781, CVE-2019-11510, CVE-2018-13379, CVE-2020-5902, CVE-2020-15505, CVE-2020-0688, CVE-2019-3396, CVE-2017-11882, CVE-2019-11580, CVE-2018-7600, CVE 2019-18935, CVE-2019-0604, CVE-2020-0787, CVE-2020-1472. Among these vulnerabilities, CVE-2019-19781 was the most exploited flaw in 2020, according to U.S. Government technical analysis.CVE-2019-19781 is a recently disclosed critical vulnerability in Citrix's Application Delivery Controller (ADC)-a load balancing application for web, application, and database servers widely use throughout the United States. Nation-state and criminal cyber actors most likely favor using this vulnerability because it is easy to exploit, Citrix servers are widespread, and exploitation enables the actors to perform unauthorized RCE on a target system. Identified as emerging targets in early 2020, unremediated instances of CVE-2019-19781 and CVE-2019-11510 continued to be exploited throughout the year by nation-state advanced persistent threat actors (APTs) who leveraged these and other vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2018-13379 , in VPN services to compromise an array of organizations, including those involved in COVID-19 vaccine development. The CVE-2019-11510 vulnerability in Pulse Connect Secure VPN was also frequently targeted by nation-state APTs. Actors can exploit the vulnerability to steal the unencrypted credentials for all users on a compromised Pulse VPN server and retain unauthorized credentials for all users on a compromised Pulse VPN server and can retain unauthorize access after the system is patched unless all compromised credentials are changed. Nation-state APTs also commonly exploited CVE-2020-15505 and CVE-2020-5902.

This group has been linked to the deployment of the DeltaCharlie malware, which has been used in targeted attacks against various sectors, primarily focusing on the technology and healthcare industries.

CISA, ACSC, the NCSC, NCCIC, and NSA recommend that organizations review and implement specific mitigations to detect and respond to potential threats associated with HIDDEN COBRA. These actions include:

1. Reviewing IP addresses, file hashes, network signatures, and YARA rules to identify any suspicious activity.
2. Adding these IP addresses to a watchlist to determine if they are associated with malicious activity.
3. Running YARA tool on suspected systems to detect potential instances of the malware.
4. Utilizing network signatures and host-based rules to detect and mitigate any malicious activity.

HIDDEN COBRA has been observed to leverage a variety of indicators of compromise (IoCs) to infiltrate networks, including IP addresses, file hashes, and network signatures. These IoCs are essential for organizations to monitor their environments and take proactive steps to enhance their security posture.

It is imperative for organizations to stay vigilant and continually update their security measures to prevent, detect, and respond to cyber threats. By implementing the recommended mitigations and remaining proactive in their cybersecurity practices, organizations can significantly reduce the risk of falling victim to HIDDEN COBRA's operations. These efforts contribute to a broader collective security, making the overall digital landscape more resilient to cyber threats.

Text: In recent surveillance, our Security Operations Center (SOC) has identified activities attributed to the known threat actor HIDDEN COBRA. These actions were flagged through the detection of malware associated with the actor, specifically the variant DeltaCharlie. To assist our team in effectively monitoring and mitigating potential threats, we recommend a focused approach on several key indicators of compromise (IOCs). Firstly, we should review a comprehensive list of IP addresses associated with HIDDEN COBRA activities. This list includes a variety of public and private IP addresses that should be added to our watchlist to monitor for any suspicious activities. Our security engineers should also leverage file hashes of known malicious files to identify any potential infections within our network. By cross-referencing these hashes with our systems, we can quickly isolate any compromised assets. Additionally, the use of network signatures and host-based rules will play a crucial role in detecting and alerting us to any malicious activities. Our intrusion detection systems (IDS) and intrusion prevention systems (IPS) should be configured with these signatures to ensure they can identify and block potential threats. The implementation of YARA rules can further enhance our detection capabilities by identifying patterns and characteristics of known malicious files. To operationalize these recommendations, our team should immediately deploy YARA rules on our systems to scan for any potential DeltaCharlie infections. Any systems flagged as suspicious should be quarantined and investigated further. Furthermore, network signatures should be applied to our network infrastructure to monitor for any traffic that aligns with known malicious patterns. By following these steps, we can significantly reduce the risk of a successful breach and improve our overall cybersecurity posture. Regular reviews of these indicators will help us stay ahead of HIDDEN COBRA and other potential threat actors. Collaboration and communication within the team will be key to ensuring that these mitigations are effectively implemented and that our defenses remain robust.

Translate the text below into German. Keep names and identifiers unchanged. Return only the translation.
Text: Threat actors have been observed conducting a persistent campaign of open-source reconnaissance and spear-phishing attempts, targeting both staging and intended entities within our organization. This campaign focuses on gathering sensitive information and preparing for deeper penetration. The threat actors are primarily interested in industry-specific details and confidential data, likely using the information to craft highly targeted and convincing spear-phishing emails. The reconnaissance phase involves the monitoring of public social media platforms, company websites, and other open-source information to identify key personnel and organizational structures. These data points are then used to tailor the spear-phishing attempts, making the emails appear highly relevant and authentic to the recipients. The aim seems to be to trick employees into clicking malicious links or downloading attachments that could provide initial access to our systems. To address this evolving threat, all employees are encouraged to be vigilant about the authenticity of emails, especially those appearing to come from known contacts or addresses. It is critical to verify the legitimacy of any unexpected requests for sensitive information or links before clicking. Additionally, ongoing training on identifying phishing attempts will be provided to enhance our collective cybersecurity awareness.
messages.output: Threatakteure haben eine persistente Kampagne der offenen Quellen-Rekognition und spezialisierten Phishingversuche durchgeführt, die sowohl Vorführ- als auch beabsichtigte Einheiten innerhalb unserer Organisation in die Kategorie fallen. Diese Kampagne zielt darauf ab, vertrauliche Informationen zu sammeln und eine tiefergehende Eindringung vorzubereiten. Die Threatakteure sind hauptsächlich an branche-relevante Details und vertrauliche Daten interessiert, die sie wahrscheinlich verwenden, um hochwertige und überzeugende spezialisierte Phishing-E-Mails zu erstellen. Die Rekognitionsbereitschaft umfasst das Beobachten öffentlicher Sozialmedien-Plattformen, Unternehmenswebsites und anderer offener Quellen, um Schlüsselpersonen und Organisationsstrukturen zu identifizieren. Diese Datenpunkte werden dann verwendet, um die spezialisierten Phishingversuche anzupassen, sodass die E-Mails den Empfängern sehr relevant und echt erscheinen. Das Ziel scheint es zu sein, Mitarbeiter dazu zu verleiten, auf verdeckte Links zu klicken oder Anhänge herunterzuladen, die eine erste Zugriffsmöglichkeit auf unsere Systeme bieten könnten. Um dieser sich entwickelnden Bedrohung beizukommen, werden alle Mitarbeiter aufgefordert, die Authentizität von E-Mails zu überwachen, insbesondere solche, die als kommend von bekannten Kontakten oder Adressen erscheinen. Es ist entscheidend, die Legitimität unerwarteter Anfragen nach vertraulichen Informationen oder Links vor dem Klicken zu überprüfen. Zusätzlich wird kontinuierliche Ausbildung zur Erkennung von Phishingversuchen angeboten, um unsere kollektive Cybersicherheitsbewusstsein zu steigern.

Example 2: The National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center (NCCIC) is aware of ongoing APT actor activity attempting to infiltrate the networks of global managed service providers (MSPs). Since May 2016, APT actors have used various tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) for the purposes of cyber espionage and intellectual property theft. APT actors have targeted victims in several U.S. critical infrastructure sectors, including Information Technology (IT), Energy, Healthcare and Public Health, Communications, and Critical Manufacturing. This Technical Alert (TA) provides information and guidance to assist MSP customer network and system administrators with the detection of malicious activity on their networks and systems and the mitigation of associated risks. This TA includes an overview of TTPs used by APT actors in MSP network environments, recommended mitigation techniques, and information on reporting incidents. MSPs provide remote management of customer IT and end-user systems. The number of organizations using MSPs has grown significantly over recent years because MSPs allow their customers to scale and support their network environments at a lower cost than financing these resources internally. MSPs generally have direct and unfettered access to their customers' networks, and may store customer data on their own internal infrastructure. By servicing a large number of customers, MSPs can achieve significant economies of scale. However, a compromise in one part of an MSP's network can spread globally, affecting other customers and introducing risk. Using an MSP significantly increases an organization's virtual enterprise infrastructure footprint and its number of privileged accounts, creating a larger attack surface for cyber criminals and nation-state actors. By using compromised legitimate MSP credentials (e.g., administration, domain, user), APT actors can move bidirectionally between an MSP and its customers' shared networks. Bidirectional movement between networks allows APT actors to easily obfuscate detection measures and maintain a presence on victims' networks. Note: NCCIC previously released information related to this activity in Alert TA17-117A: Intrusions Affecting Multiple Victims Across Multiple Sectors published on April 27, 2017, which includes indicators of compromise, signatures, suggested detection methods, and recommended mitigation techniques.

In recent variants, the server's response is parsed as a JSON document with a key-value pair, where the key is used as an AES 256 encryption key in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) or Counter (CTR) mode to decrypt the value. The decrypted data is written as a file to the system's temporary directory, as provided by the method of Node.js, and executed using the method of Node.js, which spawns a shell as a child process of the current Electron application. The text "Update Finished" is then logged to the shell for the user to see. Observed payloads include updated macOS and Windows variants of Manuscrypt, a custom remote access trojan (RAT), that collects system information and has the ability to execute arbitrary commands and download additional payloads (see North Korean Remote Access Tool: COPPERHEDGE ). Post-compromise activity is tailored specifically to the victim's environment and at times has been completed within a week of the initial intrusion. DAFOM DAFOM purports to be a "cryptocurrency portfolio application." A Mach-O binary packaged within the Electron application was signed by an Apple digital signature issued for the Apple Developer Team W58CYKFH67. The certificate associated with Apple Developer Team W58CYKFH67 has been revoked. A metadata file packaged in the DAFOM application provided the URL for bug reports. As of April 2022, this page was unavailable.

Example 2: The U.S. government has identified a group of North Korean state-sponsored malicious cyber actors using tactics similar to the previously identified Lazarus Group (see AppleJeus: Analysis of North Korea's Cryptocurrency Malware ). The Lazarus Group used AppleJeus trojanized cryptocurrency applications targeting individuals and companies-including cryptocurrency exchanges and financial services companies-through the dissemination of cryptocurrency trading applications that were modified to include malware that facilitates theft of cryptocurrency. As of April 2022, North Korea's Lazarus Group actors have targeted various firms, entities, and exchanges in the blockchain and cryptocurrency industry using spearphishing campaigns and malware to steal cryptocurrency. These actors will likely continue exploiting vulnerabilities of cryptocurrency technology firms, gaming companies, and exchanges to generate and launder funds to support the North Korean regime. Intrusions begin with a large number of spearphishing messages sent to employees of cryptocurrency companies-often working in system administration or software development/IT operations (DevOps)-on a variety of communication platforms. The messages often mimic a recruitment effort and offer high-paying jobs to entice the recipients to download malware-laced cryptocurrency applications, which the U.S. government refers to as "TraderTraitor." The term TraderTraitor describes a series of malicious applications written using cross-platform JavaScript code with the Node.js runtime environment using the Electron framework. The malicious applications are derived from a variety of open-source projects and purport to be cryptocurrency trading or price prediction tools. TraderTraitor campaigns feature websites with modern design advertising the alleged features of the applications (see figure 1). The JavaScript code providing the core functions of the software is bundled with Webpack. Within the code is a function that purports to be an "update," with a name such as , that downloads and executes a malicious payload (see figure 2).

Text: In our latest threat research, we have observed a heightened interest from threat actors in specific organizations monitored by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Although no compromises have been reported, our analysis indicates an active pursuit of sensitive information. The targeted organizations have shown interest in publically web-based remote access infrastructure, suspicious email attachments, and the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. Additionally, shortened URLs have been identified as a vector in this campaign. The threat actors' tactics have involved obtaining valid credentials, masquerading as authorized users, and ultimately compromising the target network. These organizations should remain vigilant and continue to monitor their networks for any unusual activity, particularly when interacting with unfamiliar web-based services, email attachments, and SMB connections.

messages.input:
Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: On July 13, 2020 EST, SAP released the patch for a critical vulnerability, CVE-2020-6287 , affecting its NetWeaver AS for Java component. This vulnerability can lead to compromise of vulnerable SAP installations, including the modification or extraction of highly sensitive information, as well as the disruption of critical business processes. A remote, unauthenticated attacker can exploit this vulnerability through an HTTP interface, which is typically exposed to end users and, in many cases, exposed to the internet. The vulnerability is introduced due to the lack of authentication in a web component of the SAP NetWeaver AS for Java allowing for several high-privileged activities on the SAP system. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can obtain unrestricted access to SAP systems through the creation of high-privileged users and the execution of arbitrary operating system commands with the privileges of the SAP service user account ( ), which has unrestricted access to the SAP database and is able to perform application maintenance activities, such as shutting down federated SAP applications. The confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the data and processes hosted by the SAP application are at risk by this vulnerability. CISA strongly recommends organizations review SAP Security Note #2934135 for more information and apply critical patches as soon as possible. CISA recommends prioritizing patching over application of individual mitigations. When patching, external facing systems should be urgently addressed, followed by internal systems.

Example 2: This joint Technical Alert (TA) is the result of analytic efforts between the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). This alert provides information on Russian government actions targeting U.S. Government entities as well as organizations in the energy, nuclear, commercial facilities, water, aviation, and critical manufacturing sectors. It also contains indicators of compromise (IOCs) and technical details on the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used by Russian government cyber actors on compromised victim networks. DHS and FBI produced this alert to educate network defenders to enhance their ability to identify and reduce exposure to malicious activity. DHS and FBI characterize this activity as a multi-stage intrusion campaign by Russian government cyber actors who targeted small commercial facilities' networks where they staged malware, conducted spear phishing, and gained remote access into energy sector networks. After obtaining access, the Russian government cyber actors conducted network reconnaissance, moved laterally, and collected information pertaining to Industrial Control Systems (ICS). Analysis by DHS and FBI, resulted in the identification of distinct indicators and behaviors related to this activity. Of note, the report Dragonfly: Western energy sector targeted by sophisticated attack group, released by Symantec on September 6, 2017, provides additional information about this ongoing campaign. This campaign comprises two distinct categories of victims: staging and intended targets. The initial victims are peripheral organizations such as trusted third-party suppliers with less secure networks, referred to as "staging targets" throughout this alert. The threat actors used the staging targets' networks as pivot points and malware repositories when targeting their final intended victims. NCCIC and FBI judge the ultimate objective of the actors is to compromise organizational networks, also referred to as the "intended target." DHS used the Lockheed-Martin Cyber Kill Chain model to analyze, discuss, and dissect malicious cyber activity.
