Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: Adversaries use known vulnerabilities and phishing attacks to compromise the security of organizations. CISA offers several free scanning and testing services to help organizations reduce their exposure to threats by taking a proactive approach to mitigating attack vectors. Cyber Hygiene: Vulnerability Scanning helps secure your internet-facing systems from weak configuration and known vulnerabilities. It also encourages organizations to adopt modern security best practices. CISA performs regular network and vulnerability scans and delivers a weekly report for your action. Once initiated, this service is mostly automated and requires little direct interaction. After CISA receives the required paperwork for Cyber Hygiene, our scans will start within 72 hours and you'll begin receiving reports within two weeks. CISA's Cyber Essentials : a guide for leaders of small businesses as well as leaders of small and local government agencies to develop an actionable understanding of where to start implementing organizational cybersecurity practices. If you have any further questions related to this Joint Alert, please contact the FBI at either your local Cyber Task Force or FBI CyWatch.

Example 2: During the holidays, internet-connected devices also known as Internet of Things (IoT) are often popular gifts-such as smart TVs, watches, toys, phones, and tablets. This technology provides a level of convenience to our lives, but it requires that we share more information than ever. The security of this information, and the security of these devices, is not always guaranteed. The National Cybersecurity and Communications Integration Center (NCCIC), part of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), recommends these important steps you should consider to make your Internet of Things more secure: Use strong passwords . Passwords are a common form of authentication and are often the only barrier between you and your personal information. Some internet-enabled devices are configured with default passwords to simplify setup. These default passwords are easily found online, so they don't provide any protection. Choose strong passwords to help secure your device. See Choosing and Protecting Passwords for more information. Evaluate your security settings . Most devices offer a variety of features that you can tailor to meet your needs and requirements. Enabling certain features to increase convenience or functionality may leave you more at risk. It is important to examine the settings, particularly security settings, and select options that meet your needs without putting you at increased risk. If you install a patch or a new version of software, or if you become aware of something that might affect your device, reevaluate your settings to make sure they are still appropriate. See Good Security Habits for more information. Ensure you have up-to-date software . When manufacturers become aware of vulnerabilities in their products, they often issue patches to fix the problem. Patches are software updates that fix a particular issue or vulnerability within your device's software. Make sure to apply relevant patches as soon as possible to protect your devices. See Understanding Patches for more information.

Mimikatz, a well-known post-exploitation tool, is employed for the extraction of credentials from the volatile memory of compromised systems. Its capability to bypass security measures renders it a favored choice among threat actors. In contrast, Ngrok, a tunneling software, is used to establish secure, public tunnels to local servers, enabling remote access and potential lateral movement within networks. The threat actors are employing TTPs such as T1136.002 (Living off the Land), T1090 (Actively Exploited), T1018 (PowerShell), T1098 (Command and Scripting Interpreter), and T1003.001 (Screen Capture) in their attacks. The use of these TTPs suggests a high degree of sophistication and persistence in their operations. Although no specific Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) are linked to these incidents, it underscores the importance of keeping systems updated and enhancing overall security posture. In response to this threat, we suggest implementing additional anti-virus measures, changing passwords for local administrator accounts, and closely monitoring for signs of lateral movement within your network. By following these steps, you can substantially decrease the risk of becoming a victim to these advanced tactics used by threat actors. Remain vigilant and fortify your defenses. We will continue to monitor this situation and provide updates as new information becomes available.

Text: Between mid-June and mid-July 2022, a sophisticated Iranian government-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actor breached the Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) network. Leveraging the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE), the actor initially accessed the network, then installed XMRig crypto mining software for malicious crypto mining activities on several hosts. Further, the actor moved laterally to the domain controller (DC), compromised credentials, and implanted Ngrok reverse proxies on multiple hosts. Throughout this infiltration, the actor's Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) were consistent with a sophisticated APT group. Unique indicators of compromise (IOCs) associated with this incident include specific XMRig crypto mining software variants and Ngrok reverse proxies' distinct configurations used during the attack. The compromise of the FCEB network led to the exposure of sensitive information and potential disruption of services within the targeted sectors (FCEB). Urgent mitigation measures included applying patches or workarounds for the exploited Log4Shell vulnerability, initiating threat hunting activities, investigating connected systems (including the DC), auditing privileged accounts, and assuming lateral movement by the threat actor. To prevent future incursions, efforts are ongoing to clean affected systems, secure vulnerable services, and strengthen the network's overall security posture. Post-incident analysis will be conducted to determine the initial vector of attack, identify any potential data breaches, and develop strategies to enhance the organization's defense mechanisms.

Zwischen Mitte Juni und Mitte Juli 2022 hat ein für die iranische Regierung operierender fortgeschrittener Advanced Persistent Threat (APT)-Schauspieler das Netzwerk des Bundeszivilen Exekutivzweigs (FCEB) angegriffen. Durch die Ausnutzung der Log4Shell-Sicherheitslücke (CVE) konnte der Schauspieler zuerst das Netzwerk angreifen, anschließend auf mehreren Hosts das für die maliziöse Kryptowährungsbergbau entwickelte XMRig-Software installieren. Später hat der Schauspieler sich späteral auf den Domain Controller (DC) bewegt, Zugangsdaten verändert und auf mehrere Hosts Ngrok-Reverse-Proxys implantiert. Während dieser Eindringung waren die Taktiken, Techniken und Verfahren (TTP) des Schauspielers konsistent mit einer hochentwickelten APT-Gruppe. Eindeutige Zeichen der Kompromittierung (IOC) an dieser Ereignisserie umfassen bestimmte XMRig-Krypto-Bergbau-Software-Varianzen und die besonderen Konfigurationen von Ngrok-Reverse-Proxys, die während des Angriffs verwendet wurden. Die Kompromittierung des FCEB-Netzwerks führte zu der Aussetzung empfindlicher Informationen und zu möglichen Störungen von Diensten innerhalb der betroffenen Sektoren (FCEB). Zur Umsetzung schneller Abwehrmaßnahmen gehörten Maßnahmen wie die Anwendung von Patches oder Workarounds für die ausgenutzte Log4Shell-Sicherheitslücke, die Durchführung von Suchaktivitäten nach Bedrohungen, die Untersuchung verbundener Systeme (inklusive des DC), die Überprüfung von privilegierten Konten und die Annahme von lateraler Bewegungen durch den Bedrohungsaktor. Zur Verhinderung zukünftiger Eindringungen werden Anstrengungen unternommen, um betroffene Systeme zu reinigen, gefährdete Dienste zu sichern und den Gesamtsicherheitsstatus des Netzwerks zu verstärken. Nach dem Ereignis wird eine Analyse durchgeführt, um den Angriffsvektor zu ermitteln, potenzielle Datenverluste zu identifizieren und Verteidigungsstrategien zu entwickeln.

Threat actors have been observed utilizing a combination of tools and techniques in potential cyber intrusions. The malware involved in these incidents includes Mimikatz and Ngrok.

The threat actors have been identified to employ tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) such as T1136.002, T1090, T1018, T1098, and T1003.001. Lastly, organizations should monitor for lateral movement within their networks, a technique often used by threat actors to spread within a network after initial access.

While no specific sectors or targets have been identified in this advisory, all organizations are encouraged to remain vigilant and implement best practices for cybersecurity defense. This includes regular updates, strong password policies, and robust network monitoring.

This advisory is based on analysis of available data and does not imply confirmation of a breach or compromise in any specific system. Continuous monitoring and updates will be provided as more information becomes available.

Neuerforschungen haben ergeben, dass sich die Adoption von zwei Werkzeugen, Mimikatz und Ngrok, durch diese böswilligen Akteure verstärkt. Mimikatz, ein bekannter post-Explorationstool, wird zur Extraktion von Credentials aus der dynamischen Speicherung von kompromittierten Systemen verwendet. Die Gefährdungsakteure nutzen TTPs wie T1136.002 (Leben am Land leben), T1090 (aktiv ausgenutzt), T1018 (PowerShell), T1098 (Befehl und Skripting-Interpreter) und T1003.001 (Bildschirmfoto) in ihren Angriffen. Text: Recipients: SOC Team, IT Security, Incident Response, Threat Intelligence An ongoing threat against the Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) sector, originating from Iranian government-backed Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors, has been identified. The first signs of compromise were detected in February 2022, with recent indications of activity in June and July 2022. The threat actor initiated access via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP, T1021.001). They then leveraged default accounts (T1078.001) and lateral movement techniques (TA0008) to navigate within the network. Investigations uncovered two types of malware: XMRig crypto mining software and Ngrok reverse proxies. The crypto mining software was likely employed to capitalize on computational resources, while Ngrok was used to establish a secure connection to the attacker's control server. The Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) was exploited during the attack. This vulnerability, if left unpatched, can enable remote code execution on affected systems. VMware Horizon servers, Domain Controller (DC), and VMware VDI-KMS host were the primary targets within the FCEB sector. The compromise of the Domain Controller signifies a significant network infiltration. Two IP addresses (51.89.181[.]64, 144.76.136[.]153) and a DNS query (us-nation-ny[.]cf) were observed during the attack. Monitoring these IOCs for further activity is crucial. The initial compromise took place in February 2022, followed by a CISA analysis in April 2022. The most recent signs of activity were detected in June and July 2022, prompting an onsite incident response engagement. The compromise of the organization's network, including the Domain Controller, has been verified. The assessment of the full extent of the impact is ongoing. No specific mitigations were mentioned in the excerpt, but it is advised to ensure all systems are patched against the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228), implement secure RDP configurations, and regularly review system logs for signs of unauthorized activity. Stay vigilant

The targeted sectors included the Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB), with specific attacks on VMware Horizon servers, Domain Controller (DC), and VMware VDI-KMS host.

The Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) was exploited in these attacks, which also involved T1021.001 (RDP), T1078.001 (DefaultAccount), and TA0008 (Lateral Movement) techniques. Notable indicators include IP addresses 51.89.181[.]64 and 144.76.136[.]153, as well as the DNS query us-nation-ny[.]cf.

The initial compromise occurred in February 2022, with subsequent analysis by CISA in April 2022. Onsite incident response engagements were carried out between June and July 2022. The compromise led to a network breach, including the Domain Controller, with no specific mitigations detailed in the provided excerpt.

It is strongly recommended to review network security measures, apply the latest patches for the Log4Shell vulnerability, and monitor for any unusual network activity or indicators of compromise related to the mentioned IP addresses and DNS query. Organizations are urged to enhance their security posture, particularly in relation to remote desktop protocols, default accounts, and lateral movement within their networks.

Example 1: Organizations using an HTTPS inspection product should verify that their product properly validates certificate chains and passes any warnings or errors to the client. A partial list of products that may be affected is available at The Risks of SSL Inspection . Organizations may use badssl.com as a method of determining if their preferred HTTPS inspection product properly validates certificates and prevents connections to sites using weak cryptography. At a minimum, if any of the tests in the Certificate section of badssl.com prevent a client with direct Internet access from connecting, those same clients should also refuse the connection when connected to the Internet by way of an HTTPS inspection product. In general, organizations considering the use of HTTPS inspection should carefully consider the pros and cons of such products before implementing . Organizations should also take other steps to secure end-to-end communications, as presented in US-CERT Alert TA15-120A .

Example 2: This Alert uses the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK®) framework. See the ATT&CK for Enterprise framework for all referenced threat actor techniques. This product was written by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) with contributions from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). CISA and FBI are aware of an Iran-based malicious cyber actor targeting several U.S. federal agencies and other U.S.-based networks. Analysis of the threat actor's indicators of compromise (IOCs) and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) indicates a correlation with the group known by the names, Pioneer Kitten and UNC757. This threat actor has been observed exploiting several publicly known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) dealing with Pulse Secure virtual private network (VPN), Citrix NetScaler, and F5 vulnerabilities. This threat actor used these vulnerabilities to gain initial access to targeted networks and then maintained access within the successfully exploited networks for several months using multiple means of persistence. This Advisory provides the threat actor's TTPs, IOCs, and exploited CVEs to help administrators and network defenders identify a potential compromise of their network and protect their organization from future attacks. CISA and FBI are aware of a widespread campaign from an Iran-based malicious cyber actor targeting several industries mainly associated with information technology, government, healthcare, financial, insurance, and media sectors across the United States. The threat actor conducts mass-scanning and uses tools, such as Nmap, to identify open ports. Once the open ports are identified, the threat actor exploits CVEs related to VPN infrastructure to gain initial access to a targeted network. CISA and the FBI have observed the threat actor exploiting multiple CVEs, including CVE-2019-11510, CVE-2019-11539, CVE-2019-19781, and CVE-2020-5902.

Text: The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued an advisory, alerting network defenders to the ongoing activities of Hive ransomware actors. Between June 2021 and at least November 2022, these cybercriminals have targeted a multitude of businesses and critical infrastructure sectors, including Government Facilities, Communications, Critical Manufacturing, Information Technology, Healthcare and Public Health (HPH). Over the past year, the Hive ransomware actors have compromised over 1,300 companies worldwide, extorting approximately US$100 million in ransom payments. This trend highlights the importance of strengthened cybersecurity measures to combat these malicious actors. At present, the specific vulnerabilities (CVEs) exploited by Hive ransomware remain unknown. However, the breadth of the attacks underscores the necessity for robust network security practices. Organizations in the affected sectors are urged to review and fortify their security posture to lessen the risk of compromise. Network defenders are strongly encouraged to implement the following protective measures: Implement multiple layers of defense, such as network segmentation, multi-factor authentication, and least privilege access. Regularly update and patch systems to minimize the risk of exploitation by known vulnerabilities. Deploy email and web filtering to block malicious content, particularly from unknown or untrusted sources. Employ threat hunting and security information and event management (SIEM) solutions to detect unusual behavior. Regularly back up data and verify its integrity, ensuring it can be rapidly restored in case of a compromise. Establish a response plan that includes incident response teams, communication plans, and procedures for reporting incidents to law enforcement and CISA. Stay vigilant and stay informed about the latest threats. For more information about the Hive ransomware and other cyber threats, visit <https://www.cisa.gov/rumorcontrol>. To report a cyber incident, contact the CISA 24/7 watchcenter at <https://us-cert.cisa.gov/report>.

Example 1: On August 17, 2021, BlackBerry publicly disclosed that its QNX Real Time Operating System (RTOS) is affected by a BadAlloc vulnerability-CVE-2021-22156. BadAlloc is a collection of vulnerabilities affecting multiple RTOSs and supporting libraries. A remote attacker could exploit CVE-2021-22156 to cause a denial-of-service condition or execute arbitrary code on affected devices. BlackBerry QNX RTOS is used in a wide range of products whose compromise could result in a malicious actor gaining control of highly sensitive systems, increasing risk to the Nation's critical functions. Note : at this time, CISA is not aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability. CISA strongly encourages critical infrastructure organizations and other organization developing, maintaining, supporting, or using affected QNX-based systems, to patch affected products as quickly as possible. Refer to the Mitigations section for more information about patching. CVE-2021-22156 is an integer overflow vulnerability affecting the function in the C runtime library of multiple BlackBerry QNX products. Exploitation of this vulnerability could lead to a denial-of-service condition or arbitrary code execution in affected devices. To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker must have control over the parameters to a function call and the ability to control what memory is accessed after the allocation. An attacker with network access could remotely exploit this vulnerability if the vulnerable product is running and the affected device is exposed to the internet. CVE-2021-22156 is part of a collection of integer overflow vulnerabilities, known as BadAlloc, which affect a wide range of industries using Internet of Things (IoT), and operational technology (OT)/industrial control systems (ICS) devices. See CISA ICS Advisory ICSA-21-119-04 and Microsoft's BadAlloc blog post for more information. All BlackBerry programs with dependency on the C runtime library are affected by this vulnerability (see table 1 for a list of affected BlackBerry QNX products). Because many affected devices include safety-critical devices, exploitation of this vulnerability could result in a malicious actor gaining control of sensitive systems, possibly leading to increased risk of damage to infrastructure or critical functions.

Example 2: Note: this advisory uses the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework, version 11. See Appendix A for a table of the threat actors' activity mapped to MITRE ATT&CK® tactics and techniques. Log4Shell is a remote code execution vulnerability affecting the Apache® Log4j library and a variety of products using Log4j, such as consumer and enterprise services, websites, applications, and other products, including certain versions of VMware Horizon and UAG. The vulnerability enables malicious cyber actors to submit a specially crafted request to a vulnerable system, causing the system to execute arbitrary code. The request allows the malicious actors to take full control of the affected system. (For more information on Log4Shell, see CISA's Apache Log4j Vulnerability Guidance webpage and VMware advisory VMSA-2021-0028.13 .) VMware made fixes available in December 2021 and confirmed exploitation in the wild on December 10, 2021. Since December 2021, multiple cyber threat actor groups have exploited [ T1190 ] Log4Shell on unpatched, public-facing VMware Horizon and UAG servers to obtain initial access [ TA0001 ] to networks. After obtaining access, some actors implanted loader malware on compromised systems with embedded executables enabling remote C2. These actors connected to known malicious IP address . This IP address uses a self-signed certificate CN: In at least one confirmed compromise, the actors collected and exfiltrated sensitive information from the victim's network. CGCYBER conducted a proactive threat-hunting engagement at an organization (Victim 1) compromised by actors exploiting Log4Shell in VMware Horizon. After obtaining access, threat actors uploaded malware, , to a compromised system. During malware installation, connections to IP address were observed. CISA and CGCYBER analyzed a sample of from the confirmed compromise. hmsvc.exe masquerades as a legitimate Microsoft® Windows® service (SysInternals LogonSessions software) [ T1036.004 ] and appears to be a modified version of SysInternals LogonSessions software embedded with malicious packed code. On December 15, 2020, cybersecurity researchers publicly disclosed the existence of a new strain of ransomware, Hive, affecting multiple targets across various sectors. The Hive ransomware is associated with the threat actor group known as Hive actors. CVE-2020-12812 is a critical vulnerability identified in the ransomware.

The Hive ransomware has been observed targeting various systems through multiple tactics and techniques, including Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), virtual private networks (VPNs), phishing emails, malicious attachments, Rclone, cloud storage services, and the TOR browser.

A remote attacker can exploit CVE-2020-12812 to execute arbitrary code on affected systems, leading to data encryption and potential data exfiltration. Upon successful infiltration, the Hive ransomware will encrypt sensitive files and demand a ransom from the affected organizations.

In recent variants, the server's response is parsed as a JSON document with a key-value pair, where the key is used as an AES 256 encryption key in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) or Counter (CTR) mode to decrypt the value. The decrypted data is written as a file to the system's temporary directory, as provided by the method of Node.js, and executed using the method of Node.js, which spawns a shell as a child process of the current Electron application. The text "Update Finished" is then logged to the shell for the user to see. Observed payloads include updated macOS and Windows variants of Manuscrypt, a custom remote access trojan (RAT), that collects system information and has the ability to execute arbitrary commands and download additional payloads (see North Korean Remote Access Tool: COPPERHEDGE ). Post-compromise activity is tailored specifically to the victim's environment and at times has been completed within a week of the initial intrusion. DAFOM DAFOM purports to be a "cryptocurrency portfolio application." A Mach-O binary packaged within the Electron application was signed by an Apple digital signature issued for the Apple Developer Team W58CYKFH67. Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has consistently observed Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS)-affiliated cyber threat actors using publicly available information sources and common, well-known tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to target U.S. Government agencies. CISA has observed these-and other threat actors with varying degrees of skill-routinely using open-source information to plan and execute cyber operations. CISA leveraged the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK®) and Pre-ATT&CK frameworks to characterize the TTPs used by Chinese MSS-affiliated actors. This product was written by CISA with contributions by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Through the operation of the National Cybersecurity Protection System (NCPS) and by fulfilling its mission as the national risk advisor, CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated cyber threat actors operating from the People's Republic of China using commercially available information sources and open-source exploitation tools to target U.S. Government agency networks. According to a recent U.S. Department of Justice indictment, MSS-affiliated actors have targeted various industries across the United States and other countries-including high-tech manufacturing; medical device, civil, and industrial engineering; business, educational, and gaming software; solar energy; pharmaceuticals; and defense-in a campaign that lasted over ten years. These hackers acted for both their own personal gain and the benefit of the Chinese MSS. To conceal the theft of information from victim networks and otherwise evade detection, the defendants typically packaged victim data in encrypted Roshal Archive Compressed files (RAR files), changed RAR file and victim documents' names and extensions (e.g., from ".rar" to ".jpg") and system timestamps, and concealed programs and documents at innocuous-seeming locations on victim networks and in victim networks' "recycle bins." The defendants frequently returned to re-victimize companies, government entities, and organizations from which they had previously stolen data, in some cases years after the initial successful data theft. In several instances, however, the defendants were unsuccessful in this regard, due to the efforts of the FBI and network defenders.

Example 2: Analysis also revealed that the threat actors used compromised staging target networks to conduct open-source reconnaissance to identify potential targets of interest and intended targets. "Targets of interest" refers to organizations that DHS observed the threat actors showing an active interest in, but where no compromise was reported. Specifically, the threat actors accessed publically web-based remote access infrastructure such as websites, remote email access portals, and virtual private network (VPN) connections. Throughout the spear-phishing campaign, threat actors used email attachments to leverage legitimate Microsoft Office functions to retrieve a document from a remote server using the Server Message Block (SMB) protocol. (An example of this request is: file[:]//<remote IP address>/Normal.dotm). As a part of the standard processes executed by Microsoft Word, this request authenticates the client with the server, sending the user's credential hash to the remote server prior to retrieving the requested file. (Note: It is not necessary for the file to be retrieved for the transfer of credentials to occur.) The threat actors then likely used password-cracking techniques to obtain the plaintext password. Once actors obtain valid credentials, they are able to masquerade as authorized users. The malicious script created a user account, disabled the host-based firewall, and globally opened port 3389 for Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) access. The script then attempted to add the newly created account to the administrators group for elevated privileges. This script contained hard-coded values for the group name "administrator" in Spanish, Italian, German, French, and English. In addition, the threat actors also created a scheduled task "reset", which was designed to automatically log out of their newly created account every eight hours.

Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: CISA discovered activity indicating the use of two Impacket tools: wmiexec.py and smbexec.py. These tools use Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and Server Message Block (SMB) protocol, respectively, for creating a semi-interactive shell with the target device. Through the Command Shell, an Impacket user with credentials can run commands on the remote device using the Windows management protocols required to support an enterprise network. The APT cyber actors used existing, compromised credentials with Impacket to access a higher privileged service account used by the organization's multifunctional devices. The threat actors first used the service account to remotely access the organization's Microsoft Exchange server via Outlook Web Access (OWA) from multiple external IP addresses; shortly afterwards, the actors assigned the Application Impersonation role to the service account by running the following PowerShell command for managing Exchange: The APT cyber actors used virtual private network (VPN) and virtual private server (VPS) providers, M247 and SurfShark, as part of their techniques to remotely access the Microsoft Exchange server. Use of these hosting providers, which serves to conceal interaction with victim networks, are common for these threat actors. According to CISA's analysis of the victim's Microsoft Exchange server Internet Information Services (IIS) logs, the actors used the account of a former employee to access the EWS. EWS enables access to mailbox items such as email messages, meetings, and contacts. The source IP address for these connections is mostly from the VPS hosting provider, M247. CovalentStealer is designed to identify file shares on a system, categorize the files, and upload the files to a remote server. CovalentStealer includes two configurations that specifically target the victim's documents using predetermined files paths and user credentials. CovalentStealer stores the collected files on a Microsoft OneDrive cloud folder, includes a configuration file to specify the types of files to collect at specified times and uses a 256-bit AES key for encryption. See CISA MAR-10365227-1 for additional technical details, including IOCs and detection signatures.

Example 2: Actions You Can Take Now to Protect Against BlackMatter Ransomware • Implement and enforce backup and restoration policies and procedures. • Use strong, unique passwords . • Use multi-factor authentication . • Implement network segmentation and traversal monitoring. Note: this advisory uses the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK®) framework, version 9. See the ATT&CK for Enterprise for all referenced threat actor tactics and techniques. This joint Cybersecurity Advisory was developed by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the National Security Agency (NSA) to provide information on BlackMatter ransomware. Since July 2021, BlackMatter ransomware has targeted multiple U.S. critical infrastructure entities, including two U.S. Food and Agriculture Sector organizations. This advisory provides information on cyber actor tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) obtained from a sample of BlackMatter ransomware analyzed in a sandbox environment as well from trusted third-party reporting. Using embedded, previously compromised credentials, BlackMatter leverages the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) and Server Message Block (SMB) protocol to access the Active Directory (AD) to discover all hosts on the network. BlackMatter then remotely encrypts the hosts and shared drives as they are found. Ransomware attacks against critical infrastructure entities could directly affect consumer access to critical infrastructure services; therefore, CISA, the FBI, and NSA urge all organizations, including critical infrastructure organizations, to implement the recommendations listed in the Mitigations section of this joint advisory. These mitigations will help organizations reduce the risk of compromise from BlackMatter ransomware attacks. First seen in July 2021, BlackMatter is ransomware-as-a-service (Raas) tool that allows the ransomware's developers to profit from cybercriminal affiliates (i.e., BlackMatter actors) who deploy it against victims. BlackMatter is a possible rebrand of DarkSide, a RaaS which was active from September 2020 through May 2021. BlackMatter actors have attacked numerous U.S.-based organizations and have demanded ransom payments ranging from $80,000 to $15,000,000 in Bitcoin and Monero.

Here are excerpts from real cybersecurity advisories. Study their wording and structure.
Example 1: This advisory defines MSPs as entities that deliver, operate, or manage ICT services and functions for their customers via a contractual arrangement, such as a service level agreement. In addition to offering their own services, an MSP may offer services in conjunction with those of other providers. Offerings may include platform, software, and IT infrastructure services; business process and support functions; and cybersecurity services. MSPs typically manage these services and functions in their customer's network environment-either on the customer's premises or hosted in the MSP's data center. Note: this advisory does not address guidance on cloud service providers (CSPs)-providers who handle the ICT needs of their customers via cloud services such as Software-as-a-Service, Platform-as-a-Service, and Infrastructure-as-a-Service; however, MSPs may offer these services as well. (See Appendix for additional definitions.) MSPs provide services that usually require both trusted network connectivity and privileged access to and from customer systems. Many organizations-ranging from large critical infrastructure organizations to small- and mid-sized businesses-use MSPs to manage ICT systems, store data, or support sensitive processes. Many organizations make use of MSPs to scale and support network environments and processes without expanding their internal staff or having to develop the capabilities internally. Whether the customer's network environment is on premises or externally hosted, threat actors can use a vulnerable MSP as an initial access vector to multiple victim networks, with globally cascading effects. The UK, Australian, Canadian, New Zealand, and U.S. cybersecurity authorities expect malicious cyber actors-including state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) groups-to step up their targeting of MSPs in their efforts to exploit provider-customer network trust relationships. For example, threat actors successfully compromising an MSP could enable follow-on activity-such as ransomware and cyber espionage-against the MSP as well as across the MSP's customer base.

Example 2: Three of the top 15 routinely exploited vulnerabilities were also routinely exploited in 2020 : CVE-2020-1472, CVE-2018-13379, and CVE-2019-11510. Their continued exploitation indicates that many organizations fail to patch software in a timely manner and remain vulnerable to malicious cyber actors. In addition to the 15 vulnerabilities listed in table 1, U.S., Australian, Canadian, New Zealand, and UK cybersecurity authorities identified vulnerabilities, listed in table 2, that were also routinely exploited by malicious cyber actors in 2021. These vulnerabilities include multiple vulnerabilities affecting internet-facing systems, including Accellion File Transfer Appliance (FTA), Windows Print Spooler, and Pulse Secure Pulse Connect Secure. Three of these vulnerabilities were also routinely exploited in 2020 : CVE-2019-19781, CVE-2019-18935, and CVE-2017-11882. Note: see CISA Capacity Enhancement Guide - Implementing Strong Authentication and ACSC guidance on Implementing Multi-Factor Authentication for more information on hardening authentication systems. This document was developed by U.S., Australian, Canadian, New Zealand, and UK cybersecurity authorities in furtherance of their respective cybersecurity missions, including their responsibilities to develop and issue cybersecurity specifications and mitigations.

To infiltrate network devices, Sandworm has employed the following tactics and techniques: using built-in remote management capabilities to move laterally (T1129), registering a domain for command and control purposes (T1132.002), creating new system accounts to maintain persistence (T1542.001), concealing malware within legitimate firmware update files (T1008), and leveraging valid accounts to bypass security controls (T1071.001). To mitigate the risk posed by Cyclops Blink and prevent Sandworm from compromising network devices: immediately isolate and remove infected systems to prevent further lateral movement, review firmware updates from trusted sources to ensure thorough validation before deployment, and remain vigilant in monitoring for signs of potential attacks.

Moreover, educating users on the dangers of phishing and organizing training programs to teach employees how to identify and report suspicious activity can help prevent successful exploitation. Furthermore, leveraging multi-factor authentication can provide an added layer of protection against unauthorized access.

By adopting a multi-layered approach to security, organizations can substantially mitigate their exposure to MuddyWater's malicious activities. To prevent similar incidents in the future, recommended mitigation strategies include educating employees to be cautious of attachments with suspicious names and hyperlinks from unknown or untrusted sources. Disabling macros by default and only enabling them when necessary and verified can also significantly reduce the risk of infection. Verifying the authenticity of emails and attachments before opening them is also crucial for maintaining a secure environment. These measures are aimed at limiting the vectors of attack and decreasing the likelihood of successful exploitation by the Dridex threat actor.

Once executed, KONNI can steal sensitive data, capture keystrokes, take screenshots, and run arbitrary code, posing a significant threat to targeted entities. To mitigate these risks, cybersecurity experts recommend several preventive measures. For instance, verifying digital signatures through the CertUtil certificate database tool can help prevent the execution of malicious code. Moreover, downloading remote files via the Command Prompt carries risks and should be secured appropriately. It is essential to use a text file to decode base64-encoded strings to detect and prevent the malware's entry into the system. Implementing such proactive steps can significantly reduce the likelihood of successful cyber attacks and protect sensitive data from unauthorized access.

Text: From February to July 2020, Emotet, a highly sophisticated and widespread banking trojan, experienced a dormant phase, suggesting a strategic pause in its operations. In July 2020, Emotet re-emerged with renewed activity, employing a variety of methods to infiltrate state and local government networks. The attackers mainly used phishing emails containing suspicious attachments as their entry point. They also crafted convincing phishing campaigns by utilizing URIs, user agent strings, and suspicious URLs. To gain initial access, they monitored network traffic and identified suspicious IP addresses linked to command and control (C2) servers. These servers were used to distribute updates and exfiltrate data. The attackers frequently used ports 80, 8080, and 443 for web traffic and exploited port 445 for file sharing and printer services, facilitating the spread within local networks. As a result, network-wide infections were observed, leading to the compromise of multiple state and local government systems. In August 2020, the attack landscape expanded with an increase in malicious cyber activities, complicating response and mitigation efforts. To address the Emotet threat, incident responders implemented several measures, including blocking suspicious attachments and IPs, and using antivirus software to detect and remove the malware. These actions helped to mitigate the spread of the malware and prevent further breaches. However, the continuous evolution of Emotet and the sophistication of its attack strategies underscored the need for ongoing vigilance and robust cybersecurity practices in the state and local government sectors.

Text: On December 15, 2020, an investigation began following reports of unusual network activity and system compromises within an organization in the healthcare and government sectors. According to the incident report, the attackers were recognized as SVR actors, specifically linked to APT 29. These threat actors utilized the malware WELLMESS, which took advantage of a known zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2019-19781) to gain initial access to a virtual private network (VPN) appliance. The attackers also leveraged dedicated virtual private servers (VPSs) to ensure persistence and spread laterally within the network. Their targets included user credentials, networked systems, web-based resources, a vaccine research repository, and Active Directory servers. The operations were extensive, aimed at exploiting access for broader uses and taking advantage of the criticality of the vaccine research during the ongoing pandemic. The healthcare and government sectors were particularly susceptible due to the high priority and sensitive nature of their work. Technical indicators like network traffic and endpoint monitoring were used to detect the intrusions. Network traffic logs showed unusual outbound connections and data exfiltration attempts, while endpoint monitoring uncovered suspicious activities, such as unauthorized access attempts to critical systems and the establishment of persistence mechanisms. The timeline of the incident correlated with the deployment of the zero-day exploit early in 2020, which followed the heightened security measures due to the global health crisis. The impact was substantial, as the threat actors successfully gained network access, which they then used to target the COVID-19 vaccine development process. This access likely resulted in the theft of sensitive research data, compromising the confidentiality and integrity of the vaccine development efforts. Mitigation strategies included reconfiguring endpoint monitoring to quickly identify and alert on signs of lateral movement. Regular security audits and patching known vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2019-19781, were also recommended to prevent future breaches. The organization’s response underscored the necessity of continuous monitoring and robust security measures, especially in critical sectors like healthcare and government.

The modular design of the malware enables a broad spectrum of potential attacks, including the use of SSL with client-side certificates for authentication and TOR protocols, which can complicate traceability and detection efforts. The impact of this malware is extensive, affecting the operation and potentially destructive functionality of routers, network-attached storage devices, and CPU architectures running embedded Linux. Given the severity of this threat, it is imperative that our security measures are comprehensive and updated.

To mitigate the risks, we recommend the following actions:

- Disable Network Device Management Interfaces: This can prevent unauthorized access and reduce the risk of exploitation.
- Secure Network Device Management Interfaces with Strong Passwords and Encryption: Implementing robust security measures can significantly strengthen the resilience of our networked devices.
- Upgrade Network Devices to the Latest Available Firmware Versions: Regular updates ensure that devices are protected against known vulnerabilities.
- Remove First-Stage Malware from Devices: This is crucial for fully securing compromised devices.
- Implement Network-Level Blocking: This can help prevent the spread of the malware and protect other devices on the network.

By taking these proactive measures, we can substantially reduce the risk of our networked devices being affected by the VPNFilter threat and maintain the integrity and security of our network infrastructure.

By adopting these strategies, we can enhance our organization's resilience against APT threats and protect sensitive information from unauthorized access and data exfiltration. Regularly reviewing and updating our security measures will ensure we remain prepared to counteract these sophisticated threats and maintain the security of our network and data.

- Application Whitelisting (AWL): This method limits the execution of applications to only those explicitly trusted, ensuring that unauthorized or malicious software cannot run.
- Defense-in-Depth: This holistic strategy combines multiple layers of protection to boost overall security.
- Directory Whitelisting: This ensures that only approved files and directories are accessible, thereby reducing the potential impact of threats.
- Microsoft Software Restriction Policy (SRP): SRP offers granular control over application execution, enabling fine-tuned security policies.
- AppLocker: This tool provides additional control over application execution, enhancing security by complementing SRP.
- Safe Defaults: Assuming all software is untrusted until proven otherwise, this strategy is crucial for reducing the risk of unauthorized access and mitigating potential breaches.

By integrating these strategies, organizations can significantly decrease the risk of unauthorized access and potential breaches.

Initial findings suggested that Russian state-sponsored cyber actors had exploited a known vulnerability, specifically CVE-2021-34527, to gain initial entry into the network. The actors employed tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) consistent with the MITRE ATT&CK framework, including T1078 (Port Knocking), T1110.001 (Stealthy Command and Control Communications via Protocol Tunneling), T1068 (Security Software Disable), T1556 (Service Stop), and T1133 (Modify System State).

The breach had substantial repercussions. The attackers accessed the victim network, compromising virtual private network (VPN) resources and gaining unauthorized access to cloud storage and email accounts. This breach could enable the adversaries to exfiltrate sensitive information, disrupt business operations, and result in financial losses. Although no malware was detected in the initial analysis, the sophisticated nature of the attack, coupled with the use of TTPs typically associated with state-sponsored threats, indicates a prolonged, covert operation. The lack of detected malware might suggest that the threat actors prefer to maintain a low profile, exploiting existing vulnerabilities for sustained access.

Mitigation and containment strategies have been initiated. However, further analysis and collaboration with external cyber threat intelligence services are necessary to fully comprehend the extent of the breach and develop an effective response plan. The organization has been advised to conduct a comprehensive post-breach assessment, update its security policies, and enhance its cybersecurity measures to prevent future incidents.

Develop and maintain robust backup procedures to mitigate the risk of device destruction. Conduct regular security audits to identify and address potential vulnerabilities. While there are no specific CVEs or TTPs related to Sandworm's recent activities, the ongoing threat requires continuous vigilance and proactive defense strategies.

Text: Since at least June 2019, the Sandworm team, a subgroup of the Russian military, has actively targeted network devices across various sectors through a sophisticated malware campaign called Cyclops Blink. This campaign employs techniques such as T1129 (Proxy Execution), T1132.002 (Proxy Services), T1542.001 (Valid Accounts - Network Share), T1008 (Lateral Privilege Escalation), and T1071.001 (Indicator Removal on Host), posing a significant challenge to our security posture. The primary method of compromise involves deploying Cyclops Blink, a malware designed to persist on reboot and throughout legitimate firmware updates, ensuring long-term access to the targeted network devices.

Our threat intelligence indicates that the indicators of compromise (IoCs) related to this threat, including C2 domains, IP addresses, and open ports, as well as encrypted command and control communications via TLS, have been active since at least January 2021, signifying an ongoing and persistent threat that demands immediate attention. The impact of this threat is significant, as it allows adversaries to maintain a foothold on the network even after firmware updates, complicating detection and response efforts.

To mitigate the risk posed by Cyclops Blink, we must take proactive measures. Initially, remove the malware from any affected devices by thoroughly analyzing and removing the malware to prevent its reactivation. Secondly, implement strict network segmentation and monitoring to detect any unauthorized C2 communications. Additionally, update all firmware and software to the latest versions to ensure they are not vulnerable to the same exploitation methods. Finally, enhance our threat hunting capabilities to proactively identify and respond to potential threats before they can cause significant damage.

This internal threat bulletin serves as a reminder of the evolving threat landscape and the importance of continuous vigilance in our security operations. By acting swiftly and comprehensively, we can mitigate the risks associated with Cyclops Blink and maintain the integrity of our network infrastructure.

Text: This advisory is intended to alert network defenders about recent activities linked to the threat actor MuddyWater. MuddyWater has been observed using diverse malicious techniques and tools in their operations, which include the deployment of malware such as Small Sieve, Canopy/Starwhale, Mori, and POWERSTATS. Their campaigns often employ sophisticated tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) as outlined by the MITRE ATT&CK framework, including T1071.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter - Windows Command Shell), T1027 (Create or Modify System Process), T1132.002 (Leverage Mobile Ad Hoc Network), T1566.001 (Proxy Execution - Remote to Local), T1204.002 (System Owner Determination), T1547.001 (Remote Services - WinRM), and T1001.001 (Masquerading - Service Execution). Additionally, T1059.001 (Command and Scripting Interpreter - PowerShell) is also a notable technique used by MuddyWater. The malware campaigns often involve obfuscated Base64 functions, Windows Script File (.wsf) scripts, Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) scripts, and hex byte swapping encoding schemes, which can make detection and analysis challenging. These scripts are frequently used to maintain persistence and evade security solutions. Furthermore, domain name system (DNS) tunneling is another technique employed by MuddyWater to exfiltrate data, ensuring they can maintain operational capability despite security operations. Commonly associated with MuddyWater's campaigns are the use of Telegram API for command and control, HTTPS for data exfiltration, and mutexes to ensure only one instance of a particular malicious script or process is running. Additionally, the use of PowerShell scripts and DLLs written in C++ is frequently observed, indicating a sophisticated and targeted approach. Given the persistent threat, network defenders are advised to implement robust security practices, including continuous monitoring of network traffic, using security information and event management (SIEM) tools, and keeping systems and software up to date. Vigilant monitoring for indicators of compromise (IoCs) listed in this advisory is crucial.

Top priorities include enhancing identity and access management by ensuring all users have the minimum necessary privileges and regularly reviewing and updating access controls. Additionally, we should concentrate on protective controls and network architecture, such as implementing robust network segmentation based on roles and functions. This strategy not only curtails the potential spread of any breach but also aids in isolating critical systems from less critical ones. Furthermore, staying ahead of potential vulnerabilities requires implementing best practices for vulnerability and configuration management. Regularly updating systems, patching known vulnerabilities, and conducting thorough security assessments can significantly decrease the risk of exploitation. Lastly, it is essential to strengthen our network segmentation strategies. By segmenting networks based on roles and functions, we can limit the attacker's lateral movement once a breach occurs. As we continue to face evolving threats, our security team must remain vigilant and proactive in implementing these mitigations to ensure the resilience and security of our systems.

These targeted cyber attacks have affected various sectors, including the Energy Sector, impacting Ukrainian government and critical infrastructure organizations, U.S. energy and aviation companies, U.S. government and military personnel, and private organizations, such as cybersecurity firms and journalists. The threat actors utilize diverse tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs), encompassing DDoS attacks, cyber espionage, and phishing campaigns to accomplish their goals. Their main targets are within the Energy Sector, underscoring the critical nature of their operations. For example, the 2017 NotPetya attack, originating in Ukraine, spread worldwide, causing substantial disruptions to IT and OT systems. BlackEnergy has also been associated with numerous attacks, including the 2015 Ukraine power grid blackout, where it infiltrated industrial control systems, resulting in extensive power outages. The FSB's cyber activities extend beyond destructive malware; they also conduct cyber espionage to gain strategic advantages. By stealing sensitive data, they can uncover infrastructure vulnerabilities, operational strategies, and defense mechanisms. Phishing campaigns are another method used to trick employees and personnel into accessing malicious links or opening infected attachments, thus gaining access to secure networks. To combat these threats, a comprehensive security approach is necessary. This strategy should include robust network segmentation, regular system and software updates, advanced threat detection tools, and ongoing security awareness training. International collaboration with security agencies and the sharing of intelligence can also significantly bolster the collective defense against state-sponsored cyber threats.

The incident's timeline covers the 2022/2023 school year, with the impact being most pronounced during the early months of the academic year. The compromised entities encountered severe operational challenges, with many services ceasing to function. To prevent similar incidents in the future, the report suggests prioritizing and addressing known exploited vulnerabilities. Training users to identify and report phishing attempts is also critical, given that Vice Society often uses these methods to gain initial access. Text: A recent incident highlighted a sophisticated cyber threat from malicious actors, particularly advanced persistent threat (APT) groups, targeting critical infrastructure in the United States. These actors used a range of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to gain unauthorized access to operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems (ICS) assets. The primary targets were sectors crucial to the country's National Critical Functions, including energy, water, and transportation. The cyber-attack's impact was substantial, causing significant property damage and, in some instances, loss of life. The disruption to National Critical Functions led to widespread service outages and operational inefficiencies, affecting the overall functionality of critical infrastructure. The attackers exploited their deep understanding of the target environments to evade detection and maintain a persistent presence within the systems for an extended period.

Immediate mitigations were put in place in response to the incident. These measures included patching vulnerabilities, enhancing network segmentation, and bolstering monitoring and logging capabilities. Recommendations to defend against similar threats were also provided, stressing the importance of continuous vulnerability assessments, employee training on cybersecurity best practices, and the establishment of robust incident response plans. The incident underscores the critical need for enhanced cybersecurity measures in U.S. critical infrastructure sectors. It highlights the ongoing threat from APT groups and the severe consequences of inadequate cyber defense. The recommendations aim to improve the resilience of critical infrastructure against cyber-attacks, ensuring the continued reliability and safety of essential services.

Text: In our recent analysis, we have observed a growing threat landscape, particularly concerning the manipulation and disruption of industrial control systems (ICS). Adversaries, encompassing both nation-state actors and groups with limited resources, use diverse tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to achieve their objectives. One of the most alarming tactics involves the use of TRITON malware, first discovered in 2017 and linked to sophisticated cyber operations targeting critical infrastructure. TRITON, often customized or procured specifically for these operations, can interact with and manipulate control systems, particularly Triconex Tricon programmable logic controllers (PLCs). This capability extends to Schneider Electric PLCs and OMRON Sysmac NEX PLCs, showing the adversaries' intention to target a wide range of industrial control systems. Additionally, threat actors employ resident system utilities and available exploitation tools to maintain stealth and operational effectiveness. The consequences of such operations are severe, as adversaries aim to disable safety systems, potentially leading to catastrophic outcomes. By disrupting control systems, the adversaries can manipulate or halt operations, causing significant disruptions and financial losses. To address these threats, our security team must implement robust measures. Limiting remote access to control systems is critical, as it narrows the attack surface. Using secure remote access protocols, such as those that support encryption and multifactor authentication, can further enhance security. Regular system audits and updates are also essential in protecting our industrial control systems from potential attacks.

Text: A recent incident involved a nation-state actor or state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) group that deployed ransomware against critical infrastructure, specifically targeting operational technology (OT) and industrial control systems (ICS) assets such as power grids, water treatment facilities, and dams. This sophisticated attack was designed to disrupt essential services, which could lead to destabilizing economic impacts and psychological or social consequences for the population. The attackers' objectives go beyond mere economic disruption, as they may be supporting broader military campaigns by creating vulnerabilities in critical national infrastructure. The malware used in this incident was ransomware, crafted to encrypt critical data and systems, rendering them inaccessible until a ransom is paid. The selection of ransomware indicates that the attackers aimed to cause significant disruption and use the fear of downtime to extort financial compensation. The targeted sectors, including power grids and water treatment facilities, are vital for maintaining the basic functioning of a society, making their disruption particularly dangerous. The nature of the attack suggests a well-planned and executed operation, likely involving custom malware or exploiting existing vulnerabilities in the targeted systems. The complexity and scale of the attack suggest it was meticulously planned over an extended period, though no specific Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) or Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) were identified. The potential impact of this attack could be severe, potentially leading to blackouts, water supply disruptions, and other critical service failures. These disruptions could have far-reaching consequences, affecting public safety, economic stability, and national security. The psychological and social impacts on the population, such as fear and distrust in critical infrastructure, are significant and could exacerbate the already serious technical and economic challenges. Mitigation strategies for such incidents are complex and involve multiple layers of defense, including regular system backups, robust cybersecurity training for employees, and continuous monitoring of network and system activities. However, given the sophistication of the actors involved, proactive threat intelligence and collaboration between government agencies, private sector entities, and international partners are crucial in preventing and responding to such threats effectively.

Text: From mid-June to mid-July 2022, Iranian government-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) actors took advantage of the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) to target a Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) organization. This resulted in network compromise and the deployment of XMRig crypto mining software for financial gain. The actors also extended their reach by moving laterally to the domain controller (DC), stealing credentials, and installing Ngrok reverse proxies on multiple hosts to ensure persistent access. Tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) such as lateral movement, credential theft, and remote access were employed to maintain control over the network. Indicators of compromise (IOCs) and TTPs from this campaign underscore the need for urgent action. To mitigate risks, organizations should apply patches or workarounds for the Log4Shell vulnerability, conduct threat hunting, anticipate lateral movement by threat actors, examine connected systems (including the DC), and review privileged accounts.

The attackers further expanded their control by moving laterally to the domain controller (DC), stealing credentials, and deploying Ngrok reverse proxies on several hosts to maintain persistent access. Text: In February 2022, APT actors supported by the Iranian government exploited a range of vulnerabilities and techniques to infiltrate Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) organizations. They utilized the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) and employed tactics such as Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) access (T1021.001) and the exploitation of default accounts (T1078.001) to gain initial access. The attackers then compromised VMware Horizon servers, Domain Controllers (DC), and VMware VDI-KMS hosts. To maintain persistence and exfiltrate data, the threat actors used Ngrok reverse proxies and deployed XMRig crypto mining software. By April 2022, CISA had identified the compromise, and onsite incident response engagements were conducted in June-July 2022. The compromise resulted in the complete control of the organization's network, especially the Domain Controller. Given the absence of detailed mitigations, organizations should prioritize robust security practices, including regular vulnerability assessments, patch management, and network segmentation. Indicators of compromise (IoCs) include IP addresses such as 51.89.181.64 and 144.76.136.153, as well as DNS queries like us-nation-ny.cf, which should be monitored and mitigated promptly.

The phishing emails, assumed to serve as the initial point of entry, are designed to mislead recipients into revealing confidential information or downloading harmful attachments. Upon installation, the webshells offer the attacker continuous access to the compromised system. The threat activities have persisted since 2017, with a notable escalation into early 2018. Firstly, ensure all systems and applications are fully patched and up-to-date, reducing the chances of successful attacks. This involves educating users about identifying and reporting phishing emails, as well as technical controls such as email encryption and secure email gateways. It is crucial that these measures are put in place to guard against this ongoing threat and minimize potential damage to critical national infrastructure and the financial sector.

Text: Within our network, the QSnatch malware, a notorious Trojan targeting Network Attached Storage (NAS) systems, particularly those produced by QNAP, was identified. The source of the infection was traced back to the exploitation of the CVE-2017-7494 vulnerability, a weakness in the SMB (Server Message Block) service, which facilitates remote code execution. The QSnatch malware hindered the installation of updates, making it impossible for administrators to perform firmware updates, thereby weakening the security stance of the affected devices. Upon detection, the following countermeasures were implemented: All devices were scanned to ensure no previous breach had taken place, using antivirus software and malware detection tools. The most recent updates were installed on all devices, resolving the CVE-2017-7494 vulnerability and shielding against future QSnatch infections. To reinforce the NAS devices against QSnatch and similar threats, the guidelines provided in QNAP's November 2019 advisory were followed. The investigation into the scope of the infection and potential additional weaknesses is still ongoing. Recommendations for network strengthening and enhanced security measures will be offered upon conclusion.

Text: The United States' Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has issued an urgent warning regarding the persistent danger posed by the QSnatch malware, which primarily targets QNAP Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices. Since early 2014, cybercriminals have been using this malware, with a noticeable spike in occurrences since mid-2017. The most recent upsurge was reported in late 2018, late 2019, and mid-June 2020. The QSnatch malware utilizes a domain generation algorithm (DGA), which complicates efforts to forecast and disrupt its command and control (C&C) communication. Over 62,000 devices globally have been affected since its creation, with approximately 7,600 instances in the United States and 3,900 in the United Kingdom. Given its non-discriminatory targeting of all QNAP NAS devices, all sectors are vulnerable to QSnatch infections. The malware may potentially breach sensitive data, encrypt files for ransom, and instigate further attacks on linked networks. To minimize the risk of QSnatch infections, network security professionals are strongly urged to ensure their QNAP NAS devices are updated with the most recent security patches. Regular updating and maintaining current antivirus software are essential measures to protect against this and other cyber threats. CISA advises network security professionals to watch for indications of compromise on their QNAP NAS devices, such as unusual network activity, changes in file sizes or types, or the emergence of unanticipated files or processes. If a compromise is suspected, prompt action should be taken to segregate the affected device, disconnect it from the network, and commence a comprehensive investigation and remediation process. CISA will persistently monitor the dynamic threat environment and provide updates as required. Network security professionals are strongly encouraged to subscribe to CISA's Cybersecurity Alert System to receive the most current threat information and guidance for mitigation. By remaining vigilant and proactive, network security professionals can substantially reduce the risk of becoming victims of QSnatch and other cyber threats. Upon detection of the intrusion, the following indicators of compromise (IOCs) were identified: IP addresses associated with the ACTA's operations, malicious scripts involved in the breach, and stolen credentials, which could have been utilized for initial access or lateral movement within the network. Post-discovery, immediate actions were taken to alter the stolen credentials and set up detection mechanisms and countermeasures. The networks are currently under surveillance for any indications of ongoing activity. Text: During the 2020-2021 academic year, malevolent cyber actors focused their attacks on Kindergarten through Twelfth Grade (K-12) educational institutions within the Education sector. The primary weapon utilized by these actors was ransomware, with several versions being deployed, such as Ryuk, Maze, Nefilim, AKO, and Sodinokibi/REvil. These harmful software strains were used to scramble essential data, causing operational disruptions, and requesting ransoms for the restoration of access. Furthermore, the actors engaged in data theft, compromising sensitive information belonging to the educational institutions. The disruption of remote learning services, a response to the global pandemic, due to these attacks was especially detrimental. The interruption of these services adversely affected the educational experience of students and presented substantial challenges for the involved institutions. At the time of this report, no specific Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) or Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) were identified as being exploited during these incidents. However, an in-depth investigation is ongoing, and further details may surface. Currently, there are no known preventive measures available to shield K-12 educational institutions from similar attacks. It is strongly advised that these institutions strengthen their cybersecurity stance, implement robust data backup and recovery strategies, and educate staff and students on cybersecurity best practices. This report serves as a call to action for the K-12 educational sector to prioritize cybersecurity and safeguard the valuable resources and services they offer. As cyber threats evolve, it is essential for institutions to remain vigilant and proactive in their defense against these malicious actors.

Text: Title: CTI Advisory - APT 29 (SVR Actors) Network Infiltration and Targeted Assault on VPN Device and COVID-19 Vaccine Data Storage

In the year 2020, a cyber infiltration was recorded in the organization by the sophisticated and persistent threat group, APT 29, often referred to as SVR actors. The malicious software used was WELLMESS. The infiltration started following the exploitation of an unpatched network vulnerability, CVE-2019-19781, which provided initial access. For the execution of the operation, specially allocated Virtual Private Servers (VPSs) were utilized.

The objectives of the infiltration extended to multiple network components, such as the virtual private network (VPN) device, user credentials, network devices, web-based resources, a COVID-19 vaccine research database, and Active Directory servers. Majorly affected sectors were healthcare and government, with the COVID-19 vaccine research repository seemingly the principal target, suggesting a malicious and premeditated motive. Network traffic and endpoint activity were identified as key signs of this infiltration. The network traffic showed internal network navigation, a frequently used technique by APT groups.

The consequences of this infiltration were significant, as the intruders managed to gain network entry and potentially tamper with sensitive data concerning COVID-19 vaccine research. To combat the persistent threat, the organization is recommended to fine-tune endpoint monitoring systems to identify signs of internal network navigation, thereby enhancing early detection and reaction to similar future attacks. The ongoing investigation and recovery work aim to fully grasp the extent of the breach and to bolster the network against potential subsequent attacks.

Text: Subject: Cybersecurity Alert: Emerging Ransomware Threat and Anonymizing Networks

Greetings Security Unit,

This correspondence serves to bring to your attention a newly identified cyber menace involving ransomware. The perpetrators, as yet unidentified, are employing anonymizing networks such as Tor and the Onion Routing Protocol for their operations. Their aim is to dodge detection and create secure communication avenues, highlighting the paramount importance of maintaining heightened network security vigilance.

Some indicators of this risk include IP addresses linked to Tor exit nodes, necessitating close scrutiny of inbound and outgoing traffic from these recognized nodes, as they may function as potential entryways for the ransomware.

The ransomware represents a multi-faceted danger, aiming at the privacy, authenticity, and accessibility of our infrastructure. Although the specific sectors susceptible to attack remain undetermined, given the ransomware's nature, all sectors of our operation should be deemed at potential risk. At present, no Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) have been linked to this threat. However, the continuous emergence of novel ransomware variants is a persistent worry, and we must remain vigilant in our security precautions.

As a preventive measure, we suggest the following countermeasures:
1. Block or closely monitor inbound and outbound traffic from known Tor nodes.
2. Ensure all systems are updated and fortified against known vulnerabilities.
3. Implement stringent access controls and multi-factor authentication where applicable.
4. Regularly back up critical data and ensure backups are secure and segregated.
5. Conduct frequent security audits and penetration testing to identify and rectify weaknesses.

Please distribute this information to all pertinent teams and departments. Let's collaborate to protect the security and integrity of our systems in the face of these escalating threats.

Best Regards,
[Your Name]
[Your Position]

Text: In the ever-evolving landscape of cybersecurity, an unknown cyber threat entity has consistently attacked U.S. government agencies, essential infrastructure entities, and private sector organizations, with activities beginning as early as June 2020. This entity's approach primarily involves capitalizing on various weaknesses, particularly those related to Pulse Connect Secure devices. The list of exploited weaknesses encompasses CVE-2019-11510, CVE-2020-8260, CVE-2020-8243, CVE-2021-22893, CVE-2021-22894, CVE-2021-22899, and CVE-2021-22900. These vulnerabilities are utilized to secure initial entry and deploy webshells on Pulse Connect Secure devices, thus granting the entity ongoing access and resilience. The entity's methods, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) are diverse, encompassing authentication bypass, multi-factor authentication bypass, password logging, and persistence through updates. These methods underscore the entity's flexibility and resolve to maintain control over targeted systems. Given these risks, it is crucial for organizations within the critical infrastructure sector to remain alert and proactive. Recommended defense strategies include operating the Pulse Secure Connect Integrity Tool, updating to the most recent software version, and examining for any signs of malicious activity. As the threat entity continues to develop and adapt, it is essential to stay informed about the latest signs of compromise (IOCs) associated with these attacks. By doing so, organizations can bolster their cybersecurity stance and lessen the likelihood of falling victim to these persistent threats. Stay tuned for further updates as we continue to track this ongoing threat situation.

Text: In an immediate cybersecurity alert, we highlight the continuous cyber threat activities aimed at government organizations at the federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial (SLTT) levels, as well as various private sector entities. Since mid-December 2020, unknown cybercriminals have been leveraging an unpatched vulnerability (CVE-2021-27101), which was addressed with a patch on December 23, 2020. It is essential that all affected organizations swiftly implement this patch. The criminals have been found to utilize SQL injection vulnerabilities and HTTP header parameters to penetrate networks, installing webshell malware for continued access. Upon gaining entry, they have been exfiltrating sensitive organizational data, possibly compromising confidential information, and engaging in extortion activities. Furthermore, these criminals have been meticulous in deleting log files to avoid detection. The sectors affected include healthcare, law, telecommunications, finance, and energy. Network security personnel are advised to stay alert and examine network traffic for any irregular activity related to these sectors. To minimize risk, we strongly urge organizations to prioritize system updates, particularly those using software vulnerable to CVE-2021-27101. Continuous monitoring for webshell activity is also recommended, as it frequently indicates this type of cyber intrusion. Adhering to best cybersecurity practices and staying informed is vital for preserving our digital infrastructure. We will persistently monitor the developing threat landscape and offer updates as required. As a response to this incident, immediate measures have been taken to segregate the affected systems, halt any ongoing Quasar operations, and reinforce security protocols to prevent further intrusion.
